NLD: Santos Basin is an offshore passive-margin sedimentary basin that occupies the southeastern Brazilian continental margin between the Campos and Pelotas basins and hosts major Brazilian Pre-Salt Aptian carbonate reservoirs. Covering about 350,000 km², it formed during the Early Cretaceous breakup of Gondwana and is bounded chiefly by the Cabo Frio High to the north, the Florianópolis Platform to the south, the Santos hinge line to the west, and the São Paulo Plateau to the east.

Barra Velha Formation is an Aptian lacustrine carbonate lithostratigraphic unit that forms the upper pre-salt succession of the Santos Basin and is characterized by shrub- and spherulite-rich carbonates, dolostones, intraclastic grainstones and rudstones, and Mg-rich claystones deposited in a shallow alkaline lake system. It overlies the Itapema Formation across the Pre-Alagoas Unconformity, is internally divided by the Intra-Alagoas Unconformity into rift and sag intervals, and is capped by the Ariri evaporites.

Aptian is an Early Cretaceous geologic age that corresponds, in the South Atlantic pre-salt context, to the interval of widespread lacustrine carbonate deposition followed by emplacement of a regionally extensive evaporite cover. In Brazilian pre-salt studies, the term commonly designates the time span of the main pre-salt sag deposits and associated salt succession across basins such as Santos and Campos.

Porosity is a petrophysical property that quantifies the volume fraction of void space in a rock available to contain fluids. In Brazilian pre-salt carbonate reservoirs, it occurs as pore systems such as vuggy, moldic, interparticle, intraparticle, intercrystalline, and microfracture porosity, and it is strongly controlled by depositional texture and diagenetic processes such as dissolution, cementation, and silicification.

Campos Basin is a passive-margin sedimentary basin that occupies the southeastern Brazilian margin between the Vitória High to the north and the Cabo Frio High to the south, having formed during Late Jurassic–Early Cretaceous rifting related to the breakup of Gondwana. Extending mainly offshore Rio de Janeiro and southern Espírito Santo, it contains major pre-salt lacustrine carbonate reservoirs and has been one of Brazil’s most important oil- and gas-producing basins.

Itapema Formation is a pre-salt lacustrine lithostratigraphic unit that consists of interbedded mollusk-rich coquinas, bioclastic carbonate facies, and dark shale to mudstone deposited during the upper rift stage of the Santos Basin. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly combines shell-rich reservoir intervals with organic-rich Jiquiá shales of source-rock potential and lies beneath the Barra Velha Formation, between the Jiquiá/Buracica and Pré-Alagoas unconformities.

Permeability is a petrophysical property that quantifies a reservoir rock’s ability to transmit fluids through its interconnected pore system. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonate reservoirs, it is often highly heterogeneous because flow may occur through both the rock matrix and high-permeability features such as fractures, vugs, and caves. As a result, permeability is a key parameter for estimating flow capacity and production potential, and it can be strongly underestimated if thin highly permeable layers are not resolved.

Grainstone is a grain-supported carbonate facies that lacks mud matrix and, in the Barra Velha Formation, is distinguished from spherulitestone by containing more than 50% reworked components. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it commonly comprises reworked shrubs and spherulitestone fragments, peloids, spherulites, volcanic clasts, ooids, and bioclasts, and typically occurs as coarse, tightly packed beds with variable sorting and common fining-upward patterns produced by high-energy lacustrine shoreline reworking.

Carbonate reservoir is a hydrocarbon reservoir that is hosted in carbonate rocks and whose porosity and permeability are controlled by highly heterogeneous depositional facies, diagenetic alteration, and structural compartmentalization. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, these reservoirs are commonly lacustrine Aptian carbonates in which secondary dissolution porosity is often critical to reservoir quality, while facies variation, cementation, faults, and hydrothermal influences can create abrupt vertical and lateral permeability contrasts.

Ariri Formation is an Upper Aptian evaporitic stratigraphic unit that caps the Barra Velha Formation and provides the regional seal for the Brazilian pre-salt petroleum system. In the Santos Basin it is dominated by basal anhydrite and thick halite, with interlayers of more soluble potassium- and magnesium-bearing salts such as carnallite, tachyhydrite, and sylvite, and locally reaches about 2 to 2.65 km in thickness.

Dissolution is a diagenetic process that removes soluble carbonate and Mg-clay components from pre-salt lacustrine rocks, generating secondary porosity and modifying the original depositional fabric. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly affects Mg-claystones with spherulites, laminites, shrubs, and grainstones, producing vuggy, intragranular, and inter-framework pores, often more intensely in structural highs and thereby exerting a major control on reservoir quality.

Fault is a structural discontinuity that accommodates relative displacement of rock volumes along a fracture surface or fault zone. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonate reservoirs, faults are commonly classified by length, orientation, and syn- or post-depositional age, and their fault-core and damage-zone architecture strongly controls fracture density, karstification, non-matrix porosity, and reservoir heterogeneity.

Evaporite is a chemical sedimentary rock that forms by the precipitation of soluble minerals from highly evaporated brines in strongly evaporative lacustrine or shallow-marine settings. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, Aptian evaporites of the Ariri and Retiro formations consist mainly of halite and anhydrite, with locally sylvite and carnallite, and they form the thick regional stratigraphic seal over the carbonate reservoirs.

Dolomite is a carbonate mineral that consists of calcium magnesium carbonate and commonly forms in Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates as a primary precipitate, a replacive diagenetic phase, or a pore-filling cement. In the Barra Velha and analogous pre-salt successions, it commonly occurs as rhombohedral, microcrystalline, lamellar, or saddle crystals, replacing calcite or Mg-clay and locally cementing pores, vugs, and fractures.

Spherulite is a carbonate grain that consists of a spherical to sub-spherical aggregate of radiating fibro-radial calcite crystals, typically showing radial extinction in thin section. In the Barra Velha Formation, spherulites commonly range from about 0.1 to 4 mm in diameter, may contain nuclei of micrite, clay minerals, or rare ostracod fragments, and are commonly altered by dolomitization, recrystallization, or local silicification.

Diagenesis is a post-depositional alteration process that modifies carbonate sediments and rocks through dissolution, cementation, recrystallization, dolomitization, compaction, and mineral replacement. In Brazilian pre-salt lacustrine carbonates, it is the main control on pore-size distribution, connectivity, porosity, and permeability, with processes such as Mg-clay and carbonate dissolution generating vuggy and moldic porosity, while calcite, dolomite, silica cements, and chemical compaction commonly occlude or locally preserve reservoir pore space.

Structural high is a positive structural relief element that stands above adjacent structural lows because of fault-controlled uplift, reduced subsidence, or both. In the Brazilian pre-salt, structural highs commonly correspond to horsts or faulted borders of grabens and half-grabens, persist through syn-rift evolution, and often favor the deposition and trapping of Barra Velha carbonate reservoirs.

Barremian is an Early Cretaceous chronostratigraphic stage and geochronologic age that, in the Brazilian pre-salt, represents a key syn-rift interval between older rift deposits and the Aptian lacustrine-salt succession. In Campos and adjacent basins, the base Barremian is commonly mapped at the top of the Cabiúnas Formation, and Barremian subdivisions are used to date fault activity, accommodation development, and Barremian-Aptian diagenetic events.

Silicification is a diagenetic process that replaces carbonate and Mg-rich clay constituents of reservoir rocks with silica through concurrent dissolution of calcium carbonate and precipitation of silica. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it can occur from syndepositional to burial stages and commonly appears as microcrystalline silica, chalcedony, quartz cement, pore-filling silica, or siliceous bands, increasing mineralogical heterogeneity and commonly reducing porosity and permeability.

Reservoir quality is a petrophysical characteristic of a reservoir rock that expresses its capacity to store and transmit fluids through connected pore space. In Brazilian pre-salt carbonates, it is primarily evaluated from porosity and permeability and is controlled by depositional facies and diagenetic evolution, including grain size and sorting, pore type, dissolution, recrystallization, cementation, compaction, and fracturing.

Coquina is a bioclastic carbonate rock that consists of accumulations of biological hard parts, commonly shell-rich and bioclast-enriched, and in the Brazilian pre-salt typically shows packstone, grainstone, or rudstone textures. In the Itapema Formation of the Santos Basin, it is commonly dominated by reworked bivalve shells with subordinate gastropods and ostracods, and it forms an important reservoir facies where moldic, vuggy, and intergranular porosity may be well developed.

Piçarras Formation is a syn-rift lithostratigraphic unit in the Brazilian pre-salt of the Santos Basin that records the first major siliciclastic and initial lacustrine deposition during Barremian continental rifting, overlying the Camboriú Formation and underlying the Itapema Formation. It is characterized by proximal alluvial-fan conglomerates and polymictic to coarse- and medium-grained sandstones, passing basinward into distal lacustrine fine sandstones, siltstones, shales, siliciclastic laminites, and talc-stevensite-rich claystones.

Calcite is a carbonate mineral that is the crystalline calcium carbonate phase commonly present in Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates as fascicular, spherulitic, blocky, or microcrystalline forms. In Brazilian Pre-Salt reservoirs, it occurs both as primary precipitates and as diagenetic cement or replacement, filling interparticle, intraparticle, vugular, and fracture porosity and locally replacing grains, peloids, and ooid envelopes.

Early Cretaceous is a geologic time interval that comprises the earlier part of the Cretaceous Period and, in the Brazilian Pre-Salt, corresponds to the rift-to-sag evolution during which South Atlantic extensional basins formed and key pre-salt deposits accumulated. In the Santos and Campos basins, this interval includes deposition of lacustrine organic-rich shales, Aptian carbonate reservoirs such as the Barra Velha succession, and the onset of overlying evaporite sealing that together underpin the pre-salt petroleum system.

Mudstone is a carbonate rock that consists predominantly of mud matrix and contains less than 10% grains. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it is commonly classified by mineralogical composition into calci-mudstone, dolo-mudstone, siliceous mudstone, Mg-clay mudstone, and mixed mudstone, and it typically records deeper lacustrine or locally reworked deposition with generally variable but often low reservoir quality.

Pre-Alagoas Unconformity is a regional stratigraphic unconformity that marks the base of the Alagoas Stage and the transition from rifting to the transitional pre-salt sag phase in the Brazilian basins. In the pre-salt succession, it commonly separates lower syn-rift deposits, including coquina-bearing intervals, from overlying upper pre-salt carbonates. Seismically, it is typically a low- to medium-amplitude discontinuous reflector, expressed locally as an angular erosional surface over palaeohighs but passing into a near-conformable surface in palaeodepressions.

Fracture is a planar rock discontinuity that forms by brittle deformation and creates non-matrix porosity and potential fluid-flow pathways in carbonate reservoirs. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, fractures are commonly related to tectonic and gravitational processes and are especially developed in silica-rich intervals where rheological contrast promotes brittle failure; they may remain open, be partially cemented, or be filled by minerals such as silica, dolomite, or barite.

Dolomitization is a diagenetic replacement process that transforms carbonate and Mg-clay constituents into dolomite, typically during early diagenesis in Brazilian pre-salt lacustrine carbonates. In these reservoirs, it commonly generates intercrystalline porosity and helps connect moldic and vugular pores, improving porosity and permeability, although pervasive dolomitization in some sag facies can reduce pore-throat size.

Packstone is a grain-supported carbonate facies that contains mud and micrite between framework grains, commonly comprising more than 50% reworked particles such as shrub fragments, peloids, spherulites, and bioclasts. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it is typically fine- to medium-grained, with rounded to sub-rounded and variably sorted grains, and it commonly occurs as massive or laminated beds with local plane-parallel or cross-stratification and mud-rich carbonate or Mg-clay interlayers.

Silica is a silicon dioxide mineral phase that in the Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates occurs as early replacive layers or bodies, pore-lining chalcedony cement, and late pore-filling quartz cement. In these reservoirs it commonly appears as microcrystalline silica, spherulitic chalcedony, and macrocrystalline quartz, and silicified intervals are commonly associated with nonmatrix features and locally with excess permeability.

Lacustrine environment is a continental depositional environment that develops within and around lakes and includes profundal, carbonate-platform, littoral, and marginal deltaic to fluvial zones. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly refers to alkaline to increasingly saline lake systems in which water geochemistry strongly controls microbial growth, carbonate and clay precipitation, and the distribution of bioclastic components such as ostracods and mollusks.

Lacustrine carbonate is a carbonate sedimentary rock that forms in lake environments under strong local controls such as tectonics, climate, hydrology, sediment input, temperature, and water chemistry. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, these rocks commonly include autochthonous facies with shrubs, spherulites, and microcrystalline calcite, as well as reworked facies made of their fragments mixed with clay, and they are major reservoir constituents.

Rift phase is a tectonostratigraphic stage that corresponds to active extensional deformation, fault-controlled subsidence, and associated volcanism and sedimentation during the initial opening of a basin. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it begins in the Hauterivian with basaltic volcanism over the basement and evolves into graben- and half-graben-controlled fluvial-lacustrine deposition. This phase includes the accumulation of siliciclastics, organic-rich shales, coquinas, and early bioclastic carbonates in units such as the Camboriu or Cabiunas, Picarras, and Itapema formations, before the post-rift microbialite and evaporite succession.

Stevensite is an aluminum-poor Ca-Mg smectitic clay mineral that precipitates from highly alkaline lacustrine waters, typically at pH greater than about 9, in pre-salt sag deposits. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonate systems, it commonly forms laminated clay-rich facies and may occur with calcitic spherulites or dolomite rhombs in low-energy, relatively deeper lake settings. It is commonly compacted and later partially dissolved or replaced by calcite or dolomite during diagenesis.

Stromatolite is an organo-sedimentary carbonate structure that forms through microbial trapping and binding of sediment together with in situ carbonate precipitation, producing characteristic lamination. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it typically occurs as rare columnar, laterally linked domal, or stratiform facies in shallow lacustrine settings, commonly enclosing ooid-intraclastic grainstone and locally preserving moderate intercrystalline, intraelement, and fracture porosity.

The Intra-Alagoas Unconformity is an intraformational stratigraphic surface that marks a time-significant internal break within the Alagoas-age pre-salt carbonate succession of the Barra Velha Formation, commonly corresponding to the base-sag horizon in the Santos Basin. In seismic data it is recognized as a high-positive-amplitude, fairly continuous reflector, prominent on palaeohighs, moderately affected by faults, and locally conformable in palaeodepressions; it is commonly dated at about 117 Ma.

Wackestone is a mud-supported carbonate rock facies that contains more than 10% grains within a muddy matrix, commonly including ostracod bioclasts and reworked fragments of shrubs, peloids, and spherulites. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it is typically fine-grained, matrix-supported, and massive or plane-parallel laminated, and it commonly records low-energy lacustrine deposition below storm-wave base or the return to more normal conditions after stressful or storm events.

Shale is a fine-grained sedimentary rock that is composed predominantly of compacted clay-sized particles and commonly displays high gamma-ray values and very low permeability. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, shale commonly occurs as clay-rich or organic-rich intervals associated with the deeper parts of the Barra Velha Formation, where it behaves as a non-reservoir facies and local seal that restricts fluid flow and can trap CO2. In petrophysical analysis, shale is also used as a high-gamma-ray end member for evaluating shale distribution in mixed lithologies.

Anhydrite is an evaporite mineral that consists of anhydrous calcium sulfate and commonly forms dense, brittle basal layers of the Ariri Formation above the Barra Velha carbonates. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, this layer marks the transition from lacustrine limestones to overlying evaporites and generates a strong positive seismic reflector because it has higher density and seismic velocity than halite, contributing to the regional sealing succession.

Albian is a chronostratigraphic stage that represents the latest part of the Early Cretaceous, spanning about 113.0 to 100.5 million years ago between the Aptian and Cenomanian. In the Brazilian South Atlantic context, the term commonly refers to the post-salt marine carbonate interval deposited after Aptian evaporite accumulation and overlying the Pre-Salt succession.

Unconformity is a stratigraphic surface that represents a hiatus caused by nondeposition, erosion, or deformation between older and younger rock successions. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, unconformities are key seismic and well-correlated horizons, such as the Pre-Alagoas, Intra-Alagoas, and base-salt surfaces, that bound major tectono-stratigraphic units. Their expression commonly varies from erosional or angular truncation over palaeohighs to near-conformable geometry in palaeodepressions.

Hauterivian is an Early Cretaceous geologic age that, in the Brazilian Pre-Salt, marks the volcanic-rift interval associated with the Camboriú Formation basalts and the initial development of grabens and half-grabens before the Barremian. In the Santos Basin, the term is commonly used to date the top-of-basalt unconformity and related extensional structures that underlie the Piçarras and younger rift deposits.

Lower Cretaceous is a chronostratigraphic interval that, in the Santos Basin pre-salt context, spans the Hauterivian to Aptian and includes the Guaratiba Group deposited during rift to post-rift evolution. It comprises the Camboriú, Piçarras, Itapema, Barra Velha, and Ariri formations, and it contains the main pre-salt carbonate reservoirs in the Itapema and Barra Velha formations.

Pre-salt is a stratigraphic interval that comprises the sedimentary and locally volcanic succession deposited during the rift to sag stages beneath the regional Aptian evaporite seal in the Brazilian margin basins. In the Santos and Campos basins, the term commonly denotes the lacustrine carbonate reservoir succession, including coquinas and microbialites of units such as the Itapema and Barra Velha equivalents, which hosts giant hydrocarbon accumulations beneath thick salt.

Sag phase is a tectonostratigraphic stage that follows the main rift phase and is marked by the development of a broad, laterally continuous regional depression generated predominantly by thermal subsidence. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it corresponds to a transitional continental to shallow-marine, increasingly saline interval that controlled accommodation and facies distribution in the Barra Velha system and culminated in evaporite deposition, although local fault reactivation could persist during this supposedly quiescent period.

Quartz is a silica mineral that consists of crystalline SiO2 and, in Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonate reservoirs, commonly occurs as detrital grains or as diagenetic microcrystalline, prismatic, botryoidal, or macrocrystalline phases that replace carbonate minerals and grains or fill fractures and breccia matrices. It acts as a silica cement sourced internally from hybrid lithologies or externally from basement and arkosic units, and it can strongly modify reservoir quality by occluding or locally preserving pore space during replacement and fracture-related diagenesis.

Rudstone is a sedimentary carbonate rock that is grain-supported and contains more than 10% grains or clasts larger than 2 mm. In Brazilian Pre-Salt reservoirs, it commonly occurs as a reworked lacustrine facies composed of bioclasts, intraclasts, spherulites, shrub fragments, or silicified carbonate pebbles and cobbles, typically in poorly sorted massive to inversely graded beds with erosive bases. Its reservoir quality is highly heterogeneous and depends on the dominant pore system, including interparticle, moldic, intraparticle, and vugular porosity.

Kwanza Basin is a South Atlantic sedimentary basin that lies offshore Angola and preserves Barremian–Aptian presalt synrift and sag successions composed of lacustrine carbonates, mudstones, and siliciclastic deposits. In its upper synrift interval, the basin is commonly differentiated into eastern siliciclastic-rich, central platform, and western basinward domains, with structural highs hosting mollusk grainstones, packstones, and related reservoir facies.

Laminite is a fine-laminated lacustrine carbonate rock that consists of thin parallel laminae and, in the Brazilian Pre-Salt, commonly derives from originally laminated clay-rich, probably stevensitic, deposits replaced by calcite or dolomite. It is typically composed mainly of calcite and dolomite, may preserve organic matter and minor siliciclastic grains between laminae, and can be variably affected by dolomitization, silicification, and dissolution porosity during diagenesis.

Carbonate platform is a broad, shallow-water depositional system that accumulates carbonate sediments on a structural or topographic high and develops a relatively flat platform top bounded by marginal and slope deposits. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly formed in lacustrine settings over basement highs or volcanic pedestals, where aggradation, local progradation, fault-controlled paleotopography, and lake-level oscillations governed facies distribution and reservoir architecture.

Intraclast is a carbonate clast that consists of a reworked fragment of semi-lithified to lithified carbonate sediment formed within the same depositional system. In the Brazilian pre-salt, intraclasts commonly derive from spherulitic, shrub, laminated, fascicular, or microcrystalline lacustrine carbonates and occur as angular to well-rounded grains ranging from sand to pebble size in intraclastic grainstones and rudstones.

Microbialite is an organosedimentary carbonate deposit that is produced, induced, or influenced by benthic microbial communities. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, especially the Barra Velha Formation, it commonly occurs as autochthonous porous tabular, irregular, or lenticular bodies with massive texture, relic lamination, and local subvertical branching, and is typically composed of carbonate clots and peloids fringed by fibrous or mosaic calcite.

Normal fault is a tectonic fault that forms under extensional stress and is characterized by downward displacement of the hanging wall relative to the footwall. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt rift setting, normal faults commonly bound and compartmentalize crustal blocks, may display planar to curved geometries with significant dip and displacement, and can remain active during salt deposition, offsetting the base salt and influencing uplift, erosion, and reservoir architecture.

Graben is a rift-related structural low that is bounded by normal faults and forms a subsiding depocenter between adjacent uplifted blocks. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, grabens developed during the opening of the South Atlantic, commonly trapped thicker lacustrine sediment accumulations including organic-rich shales, and occur adjacent to horsts that favored carbonate reservoir development.

Halite is an evaporite mineral that consists of sodium chloride and commonly forms the dominant salt component of the Ariri Formation above the Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates. In the Santos Basin, it is more ductile and plastic than anhydrite, so it flows during salt deformation to form thick salt bodies and diapirs. This halite-rich evaporite succession provides the regional seal over the Barra Velha reservoirs.

Camboriú Formation is a volcanic stratigraphic unit that marks the onset of rifting in the Santos Basin pre-salt and forms the economic basement through basaltic rocks, including dyke swarms. Its top is commonly recognized in seismic data as a high-amplitude positive reflector corresponding to the top-of-basalt unconformity, and it is overlain by the Piçarras Formation.

Recrystallization is a diagenetic process that reorganizes pre-existing carbonate minerals into new crystals, commonly coarser calcite, thereby modifying the matrix, cement, or bioclast fabric of the rock. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates, it commonly affects shells, micritic matrix, and calcite cements, and may either create intercrystalline or intraelement porosity or, when intense, obliterate the original depositional fabric and alter reservoir quality.

Thermal subsidence is a regional post-rift subsidence process that occurs as stretched lithosphere cools and undergoes final crustal adjustments after fault-controlled mechanical subsidence has ended. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it characterizes the sag phase, when broad lacustrine accommodation developed, residual rift relief was progressively healed, and extensive Aptian carbonates such as the Barra Velha Formation were deposited.

Ostracod is a small aquatic crustacean that commonly inhabits marine and non-marine waters and, in pre-salt lacustrine systems, can persist in relatively deep, saline, or otherwise environmentally stressed conditions where mollusks may be absent. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, ostracods commonly occur in wackestones, packstones, and grainstones, where they help indicate low-energy deeper-water or stressed lacustrine settings and are a key basis for non-marine biostratigraphy.

Shrub is a calcitic crystal crust that consists of fan-shaped fascicular-optic aggregates of fibrous to very coarse bladed calcite growing perpendicular to, and away from, the substrate. In the Barra Velha pre-salt carbonates, shrubs commonly occur as parallel horizontal layers or low domes, typically with growth axes 0.15–6.5 mm long, and may trap fine detrital grains or develop into composite crusts up to 20 mm through multiple growth phases.

Cementation is a diagenetic process that precipitates minerals within pores and between grains, binding the carbonate framework and modifying reservoir properties. In the Brazilian pre-salt, common cements include calcite, dolomite, quartz, chalcedony, silica, and barite, typically filling intergranular or growth-framework pores and reducing porosity. In some cases, however, rim-like siliceous cementation can increase resistance to compaction and help preserve pore space.

Shrubstone is an in-situ lacustrine carbonate facies that consists predominantly of shrub frameworks, typically more than 90% fan-shaped, dendriform, or arborescent aggregates of fibrous-radial calcite crystals. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, these shrubs commonly coalesce into crustal or domal layers and may include subordinate spherulites or mud, while preserving inter-aggregate and vugular porosity, microfractures, and local silicification.

Pelotas Basin is a passive-margin sedimentary basin that lies along the southern Brazilian Atlantic margin, immediately south of the Santos Basin and separated from it by the Florianópolis High. In the context of the Brazilian pre-salt, it is chiefly used as a regional neighboring basin that helps define the southern geologic limit of the Santos Basin. It formed as part of the marginal depressions generated during the breakup of Gondwana and the opening of the South Atlantic.

Secondary porosity is a reservoir pore system that forms after deposition and lithification through diagenetic alteration of the rock, especially by dissolution of Mg-clays, carbonate grains, and cements, and by fracturing. In Brazilian pre-salt carbonates, it commonly includes matrix dissolution, intraparticle, moldic, vugular, intercrystalline, intracrystalline, enlarged fenestral, and fracture porosity, and it may constitute the dominant share of total porosity in productive intervals.

Pre-salt reservoir is a hydrocarbon reservoir that is hosted in Aptian syn-rift to sag lacustrine carbonate rocks beneath the regional evaporite seal of the Ariri Formation in the Brazilian pre-salt province. It is typically composed of heterogeneous carbonate facies such as coquinas, microbialites, and associated bioclastic, intraclastic, and laminated carbonates of intervals like the Itapema and Barra Velha formations, with reservoir architecture and quality strongly controlled by tectonics and diagenesis.

Subaerial exposure is a geologic condition that places previously submerged carbonate sediments or rocks above the water surface and in contact with the atmosphere due to lake-level fall, desiccation, or uplift. In the Brazilian pre-salt, especially in littoral to shoreline settings of the Barra Velha Formation, it is commonly associated with weathering and pedogenetic alteration, dolomite-enriched exposure profiles, and local erosion or disaggregation of limestones that can contribute to reworked grainstone deposits.

Basalt is a mafic volcanic igneous rock that commonly occurs in the Brazilian pre-salt as micro- to macro-crystalline, commonly tholeiitic lava-flow successions forming part of the syn-rift basement beneath the carbonate section. It is typically composed mainly of feldspar and pyroxene, including augite, and may also occur as clasts reworked into overlying conglomerates and carbonate grainstones during uplift and erosion.

Chalcedony is a microcrystalline silica phase that forms fibrous-radial, spherulitic, and botryoidal aggregates as syndepositional to diagenetic cement in pre-salt lacustrine carbonates. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt it commonly occurs in chert and silicified intervals, lining or partly filling pores, fractures, and vugs, and may locally replace the host rock, thereby affecting reservoir quality and permeability.

Cabo Frio High is a basement structural high that forms the northern limit of the Santos Basin offshore southeastern Brazil. In the pre-salt framework, it is a major physiographic and tectonic element associated with adjacent depocenters such as the West Cabo Frio Low and is characterized by igneous rocks recording multiple magmatic events.

Evaporation is a hydrologic process that transfers lake water to the atmosphere as vapor, thereby concentrating dissolved ions and increasing salinity and alkalinity. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, intense evaporation marks the dry or evaporation hemi-cycle, drives lake retraction and water supersaturation, and favors the precipitation of Mg-silicate gels, calcite, and associated in situ carbonate facies such as shrubs and spherulites.

Horst is a fault-bounded structural high that remains relatively uplifted or less subsided than adjacent grabens or half-grabens during extensional deformation. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, horsts commonly occur as elongated basement highs, locally asymmetric or S-shaped, flanked by half-grabens and grabens and controlled by planar and listric normal faults. These highs help define the rift structural architecture and compartmentalize nearby depocenters and reservoirs.

Hydrothermal fluid is a hot aqueous fluid that circulates through the crust at elevated temperatures and pressures, redistributing heat and mass and altering preexisting rocks. In Brazilian pre-salt carbonates, it commonly migrates along faults and fractures, may mix with lake water, precipitates minerals such as macrocrystalline calcite, saddle dolomite, barite, celestine, fluorite, and quartz, and can promote dissolution, hydraulic brecciation, and hypogenic karst porosity.

Compaction is a diagenetic process that reduces the volume and pore space of sediment or rock under burial stress by mechanically rearranging and deforming grains and laminae. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates it is commonly weak and mainly mechanical, recognized by crinkled argillaceous laminae wrapped around nodules, tight grain packing, concave-convex to long grain contacts, slight grain deformation, and rarer sutured contacts, especially in laminated argillaceous limestones and grainier facies.

Interparticle porosity is a porosity type that consists of void spaces between adjacent grains or particles in carbonate rocks, especially in reworked lithologies where dissolution can enlarge the pore network. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates, it is common in reworked facies such as calcirudites and calcarenites, commonly follows bedding to produce a stratified porosity distribution, and is associated with high permeability when preserved, although cementation and compaction may reduce it.

Ooid is a coated grain that consists of a nucleus enclosed by a thin, commonly concentric cortex formed by repeated accretion, typically producing a sand-sized particle. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates, ooids are commonly coarse-sand-sized and may occur as superficial or polycomposite forms, with many interpreted as originally composed of Mg-clays such as stevensite and later replaced by microcrystalline calcite or other diagenetic minerals.

South Atlantic Ocean is an oceanic basin that formed during the Jurassic to Early Cretaceous breakup of Gondwana between South America and Africa. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt context, its opening was segmented and diachronous, with southward widening, delayed rupture in the central sector, and temporary restriction of marine access to the central rift by the proto-Walvis Ridge, factors that controlled the development of the Santos, Campos, and Espírito Santo basins.

Travertine is a carbonate spring deposit that precipitates mainly abiotically from hydrothermal waters discharged along fractures, where CO2 degassing raises pH and triggers rapid carbonate precipitation. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt context, it commonly forms fissure ridges, mounds, plateaus, pools, and microterraces, and is characterized by crystalline shrub and crust fabrics whose morphology depends on fluid-flow velocity, ion concentration, and local topography.

Drift phase is a tectonostratigraphic phase that follows the rift and post-rift/sag stages and is marked by the onset of oceanic crust formation and passive-margin evolution after salt deposition. In the Brazilian pre-salt basins, it begins around the Albian at the salt base and is represented mainly by overlying siliciclastic successions, while continued subsidence and local magmatic intrusions may influence later diagenesis and structural reactivation.

Macabu Formation is a late Aptian pre-salt lithostratigraphic unit in the Campos Basin that comprises mainly lacustrine carbonate and mixed siliciclastic deposits formed predominantly as chemical precipitates in alkaline, brackish lakes under arid conditions. Its typical facies include laminated carbonates and argillaceous beds, calcite shrubs, spherulites, fascicular calcite, stevensitic arenites, and locally reworked intraclastic or bioclastic rudstone-grainstone intervals, making it an important continental carbonate reservoir interval.

Peloid is a carbonate grain that is typically silt- to fine-sand-sized, irregular, and internally massive or structureless, commonly representing a micritized very fine to fine intraclast in pre-salt lacustrine carbonates. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, peloids are major constituents of peloidal grainstones, packstones, and siltites, and commonly occur with Mg-clay matrices in spherulstones and shrubstones, where they may be engulfed or replaced by calcite aggregates.

Half-graben is an extensional fault-bounded structural depression that develops by subsidence of a crustal block along a dominant normal fault, creating an asymmetric, commonly wedge-shaped basin. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, half-grabens are syn-rift compartments commonly bounded by planar or listric faults and associated with adjacent horsts, where they control accommodation space, stratigraphic thickening, and the geometry of rift deposits seen in seismic data.

Structural low is a structural domain that lies at a relatively lower elevation than adjacent structural highs because of fault-controlled basin architecture and differential subsidence. In Brazilian Pre-Salt settings, structural lows are mapped on basement or stratigraphic horizons as fault-bounded depressions that create accommodation and commonly favor the accumulation of fine-grained carbonate muds, Mg-rich clays, and laminite deposits.

Intraclastic grainstone is a grain-supported lacustrine carbonate rock that is composed predominantly of sand-sized reworked carbonate intraclasts, mainly fragments of spherulites, shrubs, laminites, or fascicular calcite crusts, with little mud matrix. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, these intraclasts are typically angular to rounded and moderately sorted, commonly less than 2 mm in size, and the facies may show grading or cross-stratification with local silicification, dolomitization, or quartz cementation.

Onlap is a seismic-stratigraphic termination pattern that occurs where younger strata terminate progressively upslope against an inclined or older surface. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, onlap is used to interpret lake-margin migration and relative lake-level change, and it commonly marks the draping or infill of basement highs, build-ups, fault-related slopes, and other relief created during rift and sag phases.

Accommodation space is a depositional space that is available for sediment accumulation due to the combined effects of subsidence, tectonic deformation, and relative lake-level or base-level change. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it varies from structural highs to basin lows and is generated at regional and local scales by thermal subsidence and fault activity, thereby controlling the preservation and stacking of syn-rift and carbonate sequences.

Source rock is a sedimentary rock that contains sufficient organic matter to generate hydrocarbons during burial and thermal maturation. In the Brazilian pre-salt, this term refers chiefly to the Barremian–Aptian lacustrine organic-rich shales of the Itapema Formation, deposited in fresh-to-brackish settings and commonly characterized by TOC of about 2–6% and type I kerogen, which charge the Itapema and Barra Velha carbonate reservoirs.

Intraparticle porosity is a secondary pore type that occurs within individual carbonate grains, bioclasts, or coated particles through partial to selective dissolution of their internal components. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates, it commonly develops inside shells, ooids, and oncoids, may preserve features such as microbial coats after the nucleus dissolves, and is typically observed in thin section or micro-CT because it can be below conventional CT resolution.

Sandstone is a siliciclastic sedimentary rock that is composed predominantly of sand-sized grains and, in presalt successions, commonly ranges from coarse to fine grained with current laminations. In the presalt rift-to-sag setting it is typically interpreted as a fluvial to alluvial-fan deposit in more landward basin areas, and where mixed with mollusk shells it can record episodic coarse siliciclastic input into lacustrine margin or fan-delta environments.

Facies is a sedimentological classification unit that is defined by a distinctive set of rock characteristics reflecting a particular depositional process or environment. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, facies are identified from core and thin-section observations such as texture, structure, allochemical and taxonomic composition, and taphonomic features, and they are commonly grouped into facies associations to support paleoenvironmental and reservoir interpretation.

Vug is a secondary pore that is non-fabric-selective and generated or enlarged by dissolution in carbonate rock. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates, vugs are typically mostly open cavity-like voids, commonly centimeter scale and isolated at core scale, but they may touch or connect along natural fractures or, less commonly, bedding planes, especially in silicified and fractured intervals.

Depositional environment is a sedimentary setting that is defined by the physical, chemical, and biological conditions under which sediments and carbonate facies are deposited. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it spans a mosaic from subaerial hydrothermal spring, travertine, and tufa systems to shallow and deep lacustrine settings, and locally to transitional continental to shallow marine conditions, strongly influencing facies distribution and reservoir architecture.

Salt layer is an evaporite stratigraphic unit that overlies the Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonate succession and provides an efficient regional seal to the underlying reservoirs. In the Santos Basin, it corresponds chiefly to the Aptian Ariri Formation and may range from hundreds of meters to more than 1 km thick, locally reaching about 2000-2500 m where restricted marine circulation and hot, arid conditions favored massive salt deposition.

Organic matter is a sedimentary organic component that consists of preserved biological material and microbial extracellular polymeric substances incorporated into pre-salt lacustrine carbonates. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly occurs as remnants in laminites and dark bands associated with microcrystalline calcite, dolomite, and microbial fabrics, and it may both concentrate trace elements in biofilms and later generate CO2 and organic acids during maturation.

Organic-rich shale is a fine-grained sedimentary rock that contains abundant preserved organic matter and typically accumulates in deep, low-energy lacustrine settings where oxygen-poor conditions favor source-rock formation. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly occurs in profundal or sag-phase intervals such as the Piçarras and Itapema formations and is characterized in logs by relatively high gamma-ray values and low permeability. These shales are important because they commonly act as the main hydrocarbon source rocks adjacent to the carbonate reservoirs.

Rework facies is a carbonate sedimentary facies that is dominated by grains and intraclasts eroded from previously formed carbonate deposits and redeposited by transport. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, especially in the Barra Velha Formation, it commonly consists of reworked fragments of spherulites, crystal shrubs, and hybrid forms, ranging from calcarenites to calcirudites and often showing laminations, massive textures, or low-angle cross-stratification. These facies may also contain mud, clay, peloids, ostracod bioclasts, and locally siliciclastic detritus, and they are important because some intervals develop significant interparticle porosity.

Intercrystalline porosity is a pore system that consists of void spaces between adjacent mineral crystals, commonly produced or enlarged by dolomitization, recrystallization, and dissolution. In Brazilian pre-salt carbonates, it commonly develops among dolomite crystals and spherulites, and it can be a major control on reservoir quality where interparticle pores have been reduced by cementation or compaction.

Precambrian is a geologic supereon that comprises all Earth history before the Cambrian Period, including the Hadean, Archean, and Proterozoic. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, the term commonly denotes the crystalline basement underlying the volcanic, clastic, and lacustrine carbonate succession, locally preserved as brecciated basement rocks affected by later diagenetic mineralization.

Primary porosity is a porosity type that originates during deposition and early fabric formation of the carbonate, before secondary processes such as dissolution or fracturing create new pore space. In Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates, it commonly includes interparticle or interclast pore space and may also occur within clasts or growth frameworks. Its preservation is mainly controlled by the interplay of early cementation and compaction, and it can later be partly occluded by cements such as dolomite or silica.

Boundstone is a carbonate facies that consists of original components bound together during deposition, commonly expressed in the Brazilian Pre-Salt as fine-grained domal to layered constructions with concentric internal lamination. In the Barra Velha Formation, it typically resembles stromatolitic or microbial buildups formed in shallow-water settings and may be cemented by euhedral dolomite, with porosity commonly generated by fabric-selective matrix dissolution.

Carbonate mound is a carbonate buildup that forms a nearly conical, positive-relief body in Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine successions, commonly interpreted as analogous to hydrothermal travertine or sublacustrine spring mounds. Seismically, it typically shows ambiguous margins and low-amplitude internal reflectors, and it is commonly associated with faults and fractures that contribute to excellent reservoir quality and may channel silica- and uranium-rich hydrothermal fluids.

Micrite is a fine-grained carbonate facies that consists predominantly of microcrystalline carbonate mud deposited as pelagic background sediment in the deeper, calm, and undisturbed parts of Pre-Salt lacustrine systems. In the Barra Velha Formation of the Santos Basin, it commonly occurs as laminated or massive micrite, with laminated varieties showing regular light-dark layering, and its reservoir space is typically dominated by low-angle fractures rather than abundant primary porosity.

Cretaceous is a geologic period that spans approximately 145 to 66 million years ago and includes the Early South Atlantic rifting and Aptian lacustrine carbonate deposition associated with Brazilian Pre-Salt basins. In the Pre-Salt context, the Early Cretaceous marks continental breakup and the formation of lacustrine basins such as Santos, Campos, and Espírito Santo, while Late Cretaceous strata commonly constitute part of the overlying post-salt sedimentary overburden.

Carbonate rock is a sedimentary rock that is composed predominantly of carbonate minerals and occurs as either particulate depositional fabric or biologically constructed fabric. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, carbonate rocks are highly reactive and heterogeneous because syngenetic and diagenetic processes such as cementation, dissolution, dolomitization, and silicification can strongly modify their texture, mineralogy, and pore network, making them major reservoir rocks.

Kerolite is a magnesium-rich clay mineral that occurs as a principal authigenic Mg-clay in Aptian pre-salt lacustrine carbonate facies of the Santos Basin. In the Barra Velha reservoir succession, it is common in Mg-claystones, intraclastic grainstones, fascicular calcite crusts, and laminites, and its abundance generally increases upward into Units 2 and 1, reaching its highest proportions in Unit 1.

Hydrothermal activity is a set of geological processes that redistributes heat and mass through the lateral and vertical circulation of hot fluids under variable temperatures and pressures. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates, it is commonly focused along faults or other high-heat-flow pathways, where it causes hydrothermal alteration, promotes mineral precipitation or dissolution, and locally modifies reservoir quality.

A lacustrine carbonate reservoir is a carbonate reservoir that is developed in carbonate successions deposited in lake environments and whose storage and flow capacity are controlled by strong facies and diagenetic heterogeneity. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, these reservoirs occur beneath thick evaporites in the Santos and Campos basins and commonly comprise shrubstone, grainstone, laminated micrite, and massive micrite. Their reservoir quality is typically governed by secondary porosity, especially intergranular, dissolution, and intercrystalline pores, with fractures locally enhancing permeability.

Brazilian pre-salt is an offshore stratigraphic and petroleum domain that comprises Aptian lacustrine carbonate reservoirs deposited during the South Atlantic rift-sag breakup and buried beneath a thick regional evaporite seal. It occurs mainly in ultra-deep waters of the Santos and Campos basins of southeastern Brazil, where the overlying salt, commonly assigned to the Ariri Formation, seals giant oil and gas accumulations and contributes to strong reservoir heterogeneity.

Post-rift phase is a tectonostratigraphic stage that succeeds active rifting and is dominated by basinwide thermal subsidence, producing broadly tabular strata that drape earlier rift relief. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it corresponds mainly to the Aptian sag interval, marked by deposition of Barra Velha microbialitic and other lacustrine carbonates in a shallow alkaline endorheic system, followed by the evaporites of the Ariri Formation during the transition from continental to more marine conditions.

Vuggy porosity is a carbonate pore type that consists of dissolution-related cavities larger than the particles composing the rock. In Brazilian Pre-Salt reservoirs, it commonly occurs across multiple observation scales and may dominate facies such as calcirudites and shrubstones, but because many vugs are partially isolated, it can contribute significant porosity while providing little permeability, especially in silicified intervals.

Late Aptian is a chronostratigraphic interval that forms the final part of the Aptian Stage and, in the Brazilian Pre-Salt, marks the transition from late syn-rift lacustrine deposition to sag/post-rift conditions associated with the base-salt surface. It is commonly linked to depth-dependent extension that created accommodation for the upper Aptian pre-salt succession and the overlying thick evaporite sequence, although the absolute age assigned to this interval remains debated in the South Atlantic literature.

Moldic porosity is a secondary porosity type that comprises voids formed by dissolution of primary or diagenetic constituents, preserving the external shape of the removed grains or bioclasts. In Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates, it is common in bioclastic grainstones and rudstones, where it may provide good total porosity but typically low permeability unless the molds are enlarged and connected into vuggy pores or occur with interparticle porosity.

Limestone is a sedimentary carbonate rock that consists predominantly of calcium carbonate, commonly as calcite, formed by chemical, microbial, or bioclastic accumulation and lithification. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, especially in the Barra Velha Formation, limestones commonly include shrub- and spherulite-rich facies, as well as bioclastic and locally silicified varieties, whose textures reflect depositional setting and diagenetic overprint.

Conglomerate is a coarse-grained clastic sedimentary rock that contains rounded to subrounded clasts larger than 2 mm within a finer matrix or cement. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, conglomerates commonly record proximal synrift to sag deposition related to footwall uplift and erosion, forming massive or upward-fining beds in fluvial to alluvial-fan settings and including basement, basalt, limestone, or silica clasts.

Reworking is a sedimentary process that erodes, transports, and redeposits previously formed carbonate grains or deposits, commonly producing abrasion, fragmentation, disarticulation, and multicyclic recycling of particles. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it is recognized by features such as bioclasts enclosed in intraclasts or acting as ooid nuclei, mixing of components from different depositional settings, and redeposition driven by waves, currents, internal waves, or gravity.

Fault reactivation is a tectonic process that renews displacement on a pre-existing fault during a later deformation phase, reusing inherited fault architecture and sometimes producing inversion or related secondary fault sets. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it is recognized by the continuity and colinearity of early and late syn-rift faults and can generate extensional folding or increased vertical displacement, thereby controlling accommodation, depocenter distribution, Barra Velha facies and reservoir quality, salt movement, and hydrocarbon migration.

Eodiagenesis is an early diagenetic stage that affects sediments at or near the depositional surface before significant burial, producing near-surface dissolution, replacement, and cementation. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates, it commonly involves meteoric or vadose alteration, dissolution of magnesian clays or bioclasts, replacement by calcite, dolomite, or silica, and early cementation and compaction, which can either generate secondary porosity or occlude primary pores.

Dolostone is a carbonate sedimentary rock that is composed predominantly of dolomite, commonly occurring in the Brazilian Pre-Salt as dolomite rhombs and blocky dolomite aggregates within matrices of Mg-clays, organic matter, and detrital clasts. In Pre-Salt reservoirs, it commonly forms a subordinate diagenetic facies associated with pervasive dolomitization and silicification, may be interlaminated with or host chert, and can develop intercrystalline and vugular porosity that supports high reservoir quality.

Microporosity is a porosity class that consists of micrometer-scale pores and pore throats, commonly generated in Brazilian pre-salt lacustrine carbonates by diagenetic cementation, replacement, or dissolution within shrubs, spherulites, and calcite crusts. In the pre-salt reservoirs of the Santos and Campos basins, microporosity commonly dominates the pore-size distribution, tends to retain high irreducible water saturation, and has little positive influence on permeability even where total porosity is appreciable.

Late Jurassic is a geologic time interval that represents the final part of the Jurassic Period, immediately preceding the Early Cretaceous. In the Brazilian pre-salt context, it corresponds to the onset of South Atlantic extension and is locally associated with the earliest rift-related deposition and magmatism, including Kimmeridgian units and tectonic activity near the Jurassic–Cretaceous transition.

Petroleum system is a geologic system that comprises the genetically related source rocks, migration pathways, reservoirs, seals, traps, and timing conditions necessary for hydrocarbons to be generated, migrate, accumulate, and be preserved. In the Brazilian pre-salt, this system is strongly controlled by basement configuration, with source rocks concentrated in structural lows, carbonate reservoirs preferentially developed over positive topography, and major faults acting as conduits for hydrocarbons and mantle-derived CO2.

Hydrothermal alteration is a diagenetic process that modifies pre-existing carbonate rocks through the circulation of hot fluids, producing physicochemical changes and characteristic hydrothermal mineral precipitates. In Brazilian Pre-Salt reservoirs, it is commonly linked to fault-controlled fluid flow and is recognized by minerals such as macrocrystalline calcite, saddle dolomite, barite, celestine, and fluorite, locally also promoting dissolution and karstic porosity.

Alkaline lake is a lake that contains waters of unusually high pH and alkalinity, commonly enriched in dissolved carbonate-bicarbonate species and often salinity, thereby favoring chemical precipitation of carbonate and silicate minerals. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt context, these lakes were locally hyper-alkaline, with alkalinity enhanced by evaporation, hydrothermal or CO2-rich inputs, and episodic freshwater inflow, conditions that promoted chemogenic carbonate deposition and commonly inhibited metazoan life.

Tupi Field is a giant pre-salt petroleum field in the Santos Basin that lies offshore Brazil on the Santos Basin External High and is chiefly reservoirized in the Aptian lacustrine carbonates of the Barra Velha Formation. Discovered in 2006 in ultradeep water, it is one of the world-class Brazilian pre-salt accumulations, with its main reservoirs deposited during the post-rift sag phase and filling inherited rift relief.

Reservoir heterogeneity is a reservoir characteristic that consists of spatial variations in facies and petrophysical properties, especially porosity and permeability, which create vertical and lateral contrasts in fluid flow behavior. In Brazilian pre-salt carbonates, it is mainly generated by depositional cyclicity and facies stacking, structural features such as faults, and diagenetic modification including dissolution, silicification, and dolomitization. These contrasts can produce flow barriers or baffles, reduce hydrocarbon displacement efficiency, and locally compartmentalize pressure and fluids.

Basement is a pre-sedimentary crustal substrate that forms the structural foundation beneath the overlying sedimentary succession. In the Brazilian pre-salt, the top of the basement is the seismic horizon that bounds the acoustic basement and is commonly organized into horsts, grabens, and half-grabens, where inherited basement composition and fabric strongly control rift faulting and the accommodation of overlying carbonates.

Coqueiros Formation is a Lower Cretaceous rift-phase stratigraphic formation in the northern Campos Basin that is composed mainly of lacustrine bioclastic carbonates, especially bivalve-rich rudstones and grainstones known as coquinas, intercalated with organic shales. It forms an important Brazilian pre-salt reservoir unit, locally interfingers with proximal clastic sediments of the Itabapoana Formation, and is regarded as the Campos Basin equivalent of the Itapema Formation in the Santos Basin.

Bioclastic grainstone is a grain-supported bioclastic limestone that is composed mainly of carbonate skeletal grains smaller than 2 mm, typically bivalve, ostracod, and gastropod fragments, and lacks a mud matrix. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly occurs as a massive to slightly laminated coquina facies with chaotic to subparallel bioclast orientation and is commonly altered by recrystallization, dissolution, dolomitization, or silicification.

Búzios Field is a supergiant pre-salt oil and gas field that is located on the Outer High of the northern Santos Basin, about 180 km offshore Rio de Janeiro in ultra-deep water, and is hosted mainly in Barremian–Aptian lacustrine carbonate reservoirs. Discovered in 2010, it is one of the world’s largest ultra-deepwater hydrocarbon accumulations and a key producing asset of Brazil’s pre-salt province, covering about 852 km² with estimated reserves near 29–30 billion barrels of oil.

Late Cretaceous is a geologic time interval that comprises the younger subdivision of the Cretaceous Period, extending from about 100.5 to 66 million years ago. In the Brazilian pre-salt context, it commonly refers to the post-salt sedimentary overburden above the Aptian evaporites and lacustrine carbonates, represented largely by thick siliciclastic-dominated successions.

Carbonate is a sedimentary rock that is composed predominantly of carbonate minerals and forms by in-situ precipitation, biological construction, or accumulation of carbonate particles. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, carbonates constitute the main reservoir facies and include lithologies such as grainstones, stromatolites, laminites, and spherulitites, commonly with calcitic and dolomitic compositions whose depositional and accumulation rates strongly control platform thickness and facies distribution.

A pre-salt carbonate reservoir is a hydrocarbon reservoir that consists of lacustrine carbonate rocks deposited during the syn-rift to sag phases beneath the Aptian salt of the Brazilian pre-salt basins. It commonly includes microbialites, coquinas, bioclastic and intraclastic grainstones or rudstones, shrubstones, and micritic facies, and its porosity and permeability are highly heterogeneous because of dissolution, intercrystalline and intergranular pores, fractures, and diagenetic overprints such as dolomitization and silicification.

Lithofacies is a sedimentary facies unit that is defined by the distinctive lithologic and petrographic characteristics of a rock body. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt Barra Velha carbonates, lithofacies are commonly used to distinguish in-situ or autochthonous facies, such as shrubstone, spherulitic facies, and mudstone, from reworked or allochthonous facies, such as calcarenite and calcirudite, to relate depositional texture and reworking to reservoir quality.

Karstification is a carbonate diagenetic dissolution process that generates secondary porosity by chemically removing rock and forming features such as vugs, dissolution channels, caves, and karst breccias. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly develops as hypogenic or penecontemporaneous karst, often focused along faults, fractures, or cycle tops, and can markedly enhance reservoir quality by creating high-permeability pathways. If dissolution becomes too intense, cavity collapse and sediment infill can disorder the pore system and reduce reservoir quality.

Alluvial fan is a subaerial sedimentary depositional body that forms where sediment-laden flows emerge from a confined upland channel or fault-scarp catchment and spread onto a basin margin as a fan-shaped wedge. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt rift setting, alluvial fans commonly occupied arid to semiarid lake margins along normal faults, and where they prograded into standing water they could pass basinward into fan deltas and supply shoreline deposits later reworked by waves.

Calcite spherulite is a spherical to sub-spherical calcite aggregate that is composed of radiating fibrous crystals showing fibro-radial texture and radial extinction, typically at millimetric scale in Brazilian pre-salt lacustrine carbonates. It commonly occurs as a major facies or diagenetic constituent replacing stevensitic or clay-rich matrix, may contain rare nuclei of micrite, clay minerals, or ostracod fragments, and is commonly recrystallized, dolomitized, or partially replaced by chalcedony and microquartz.

Spherulitestone is an autochthonous lacustrine carbonate rock that is composed predominantly of spherical to subspherical spherulites made of fibro-radial calcite aggregates, commonly around a micritic nucleus. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it typically contains more than 90% spherulites, shows grainstone-like packing despite being in situ, and may occur in laminated, massive, shrubby, or muddy variants as spherulite size and mud content change.

Valanginian is an Early Cretaceous geologic age that marks the earliest syn-rift tectono-stratigraphic interval recognized in many Brazilian pre-salt basin reconstructions. In this context, it corresponds to the beginning of Valanginian–Barremian depocenter development, characterized by the early profusion of half-grabens, high accommodation creation, and lacustrine sedimentation associated with the initial stages of the Itapema Formation.

Depocenter is a structurally controlled basin low that contains the greatest accommodation space and sediment accumulation within a given stratigraphic interval. In the Brazilian pre-salt syn-rift, depocenters commonly form in fault-bounded hanging-wall lows between structural highs, and their migration reflects shifts in tectonic control, sediment-thickness distribution, and the preservation of reservoir-scale stratigraphic architecture.

Chert is a silica-rich rock that is composed mainly of microcrystalline quartz and, in pre-salt lacustrine successions, forms by syndepositional to early diagenetic silica precipitation associated with microbial growth or by replacive silicification. It commonly occurs as microbial boundstones on topographic highs, as thin beds in micritic sag-platform intervals, and as a major reservoir facies in isolated buildups where chalcedony and quartz cements coexist with residual vuggy porosity and fractures.

Seal is a low-permeability geological unit that prevents or strongly retards the migration of hydrocarbons and other subsurface fluids, allowing their accumulation in a reservoir. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, the regional seal is commonly provided by the Ariri Formation evaporites, mainly halite and anhydrite, although low-permeability micritic intervals and the integrity of faults through the salt can also control local sealing and leakage behavior.

Volcanic rock is an igneous rock that forms by the cooling and solidification of magma or lava at or near the Earth’s surface. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly occurs as altered volcanic fragments or volcanic-related sediments reworked with lacustrine carbonates, locally contributing clasts within packstones, calcirudites, and mixed reworked deposits.

Gondwana is a paleo-supercontinent that united South America, Africa, Antarctica, Australia, India, and associated crustal blocks before its Mesozoic breakup. In the context of the Brazilian Pre-Salt, the fragmentation of Gondwana drove South Atlantic rifting and generated the restricted lacustrine basins in which Aptian carbonate reservoirs were deposited.

Salinity is a geochemical parameter that quantifies the concentration of dissolved salts in formation water or trapped aqueous fluid inclusions. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonate reservoirs, it is commonly expressed as wt% NaCl equivalent, g/L, or ppm and is used to characterize highly saline brines, detect fluid mixing, and interpret diagenetic and reservoir evolution.

Transfer zone is a structural accommodation zone that laterally transfers displacement between adjacent rift fault segments or depocentres. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly appears as an oblique, relatively elevated structural high between surrounding lows, where lower accommodation contrasts with adjacent depocentres and strongly influences palaeorelief, sediment thickness, and the distribution and quality of syn-rift lacustrine carbonate reservoirs.

Erosion is a geological surface process that removes, truncates, and reworks exposed rock or sediment by physical and chemical action. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly affected basement highs and exposed lacustrine carbonate deposits during synrift to sag exposure or low lake-level episodes, producing erosion surfaces with truncated reflectors and generating reworked sediment from the breakdown of shrub and spherulitic facies.

Ribeira Belt is a Neoproterozoic to Cambrian orogenic belt that consists of amalgamated granitic and gneissic terranes formed in a lithospheric convergence zone during the Brasiliano–Pan-African assembly of Gondwana. In the Brazilian pre-salt context, its inherited mainly NE-trending structural fabric continues beneath the Santos Basin and strongly controls rift architecture, strike-slip and shear-zone reactivation, structural highs, and the distribution and compartmentalization of carbonate reservoirs.

Saddle dolomite is a diagenetic dolomite cement that displays coarse anhedral to subhedral prismatic crystals with curved crystal faces and sweeping extinction, commonly precipitating as fracture infill or overgrowths in Pre-Salt carbonates. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it occurs across several facies but is more strongly controlled by structural setting than by depositional facies, and its association with fractures may indicate hydrothermal-fluid influence without being diagnostic of hydrothermal alteration by itself.

Lagoa Feia Group is a Lower Cretaceous pre-salt stratigraphic group that unconformably overlies the Cabiúnas Formation in the Campos Basin and encompasses the rift to post-rift nonmarine to transitional succession up to the evaporites of the Retiro Formation. Ranging from the Barremian to the Late Aptian, it includes siliciclastic, coquina, lacustrine carbonate, and evaporitic deposits that form key seismic-stratigraphic markers and host important pre-salt carbonate reservoirs.

Pore system is a network of void spaces in a rock that includes the types, sizes, distribution, geometry, and connectivity of pores and pore conduits that control fluid storage and flow. In Brazilian pre-salt carbonates, it is typically multiscale and highly heterogeneous, reflecting both depositional fabric and diagenetic modification such as compaction, cementation, dissolution, and fracturing. It may comprise pore types such as growth-framework, intercrystalline, interparticle, vuggy, and fracture-related pores, locally forming laterally and vertically connected enlarged pore bodies.

Espírito Santo Basin is a marginal sedimentary basin that occupies the southeastern Brazilian Atlantic margin, immediately north of the Campos Basin and separated from it by the Vitória High. It developed during the Early Cretaceous rifting associated with the breakup of Gondwana and is commonly grouped with the Campos and Santos basins within the Greater Campos Basin, an important regional framework for Brazilian pre-salt stratigraphy and petroleum systems.

Fault block is a structural block of crust or older strata that is bounded and displaced by faults, commonly becoming tilted in extensional settings. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, tilted fault blocks of volcanic or sedimentary basement form crests, dip slopes, and escarpment slopes onto which the Barra Velha Formation onlaps, thereby controlling stratigraphic thickness and the distribution of grainstone and associated lacustrine facies.

Gypsum is an evaporite mineral that consists of hydrated calcium sulfate and precipitates from sulfate-rich saline waters. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, early gypsum is notably absent from the Barra Velha lacustrine carbonates, supporting a non-marine interpretation, but it may locally fill dissolution fractures and is widespread in the overlying Ariri Formation.

Clinoform is a depositional stratal geometry that forms the inclined, basinward-dipping part of a prograding margin between shallow topsets and deeper bottomsets. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, clinoforms are commonly identified on seismic data as sigmoid, concave-up, or exponential reflectors that prograde from carbonate-platform or tilted-block margins into adjacent lacustrine depressions, recording phases of progradation, aggradation, and local onlap.

Breccia is a fragmented rock that is composed of angular intraclasts generated by in situ cracking, faulting, collapse, or resedimentation. In Brazilian pre-salt carbonates, it occurs as clast-supported or matrix-supported varieties, is distinguished from conglomerate by its intraclast-only composition, and may contain interclast vugs that create excess permeability.

Clay mineral is a fine-grained phyllosilicate mineral that constitutes the mud fraction of Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates and is commonly dominated by Mg-rich species such as kerolite, mixed-layer kerolite/Mg-smectite, Mg-smectite, and sepiolite. In the Barra Velha and related Aptian reservoirs, these minerals occur dispersed between siliciclastic grains or in very thin laminae, with minor illite, illite-smectite, kaolinite, and chlorite also present.

Microbial carbonate is a carbonate rock that forms through the direct or indirect mediation of microbial communities, recording calcified bacterial-algal mats, biofilms, or microbially induced carbonate precipitation. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly occurs as microbialite facies with clotted or peloidal textures, relic lamination, and fibrous calcite, and it can form important reservoir intervals.

Pyrite is an iron sulfide mineral that occurs as a common diagenetic product in Brazilian Pre-Salt rocks, forming cubic to micro- or macrocrystalline aggregates that fill fractures and veins or replace grains, matrix, and carbonate phases. In these carbonate reservoirs it is commonly associated with silica and dolomite, may develop in organic- and clay-rich rocks through thermochemical sulfate reduction, and fracture-filling pyrite can indicate remobilization during diagenesis.

Sag basin is a post-rift sedimentary basin that develops as a broad, laterally continuous regional depression mainly through thermal subsidence after active rifting has waned. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it corresponds to the Aptian transitional section, when reduced tectonic activity allowed deposition of the Barra Velha non-marine to shallow-water carbonates and the overlying Ariri evaporite seal before full drift-stage conditions were established.

Crystal shrub is a calcitic carbonate shrub fabric that consists of in situ, fan- to dendritic aggregates of dense-radiating fibrous or bladed crystals formed mainly by abiotic mineral precipitation. In the Barra Velha Formation, crystal shrubs form millimeter- to centimeter-scale lacustrine crusts or layers that may coalesce horizontally and vertically, with interstitial spaces variably cemented and locally preserving significant primary porosity.

Calcilutite is a fine-grained clastic or hybrid carbonate rock that is composed predominantly of carbonate mud- to silt-sized material, with ortho- or allochemical grains and less than 50% siliciclastic content. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly occurs as laminated, peloidal to microbial, strongly recrystallized lithofacies and is typically mineralized by calcite or magnesian calcite with variable dolomite and quartz introduced by dolomitization and silicification.

Aragonite is a metastable calcium carbonate mineral that commonly constitutes the original mineralogy of shells and some lacustrine carbonate components in pre-salt reservoirs and is readily transformed by dissolution or neomorphism to calcite. In Brazilian pre-salt carbonates, the diagenetic fate of aragonitic bivalves, gastropods, and possible spherulitic constituents strongly influences moldic porosity, preservation of interparticle porosity, and reservoir permeability.

Alagoas stage is a local Lower Cretaceous chronostratigraphic stage that encompasses the deposition of the Barra Velha and Ariri formations in the Brazilian pre-salt succession, broadly correlating with ostracod biozone 011 and the Aptian. In the Santos Basin, it provides the principal temporal framework for the Barra Velha lacustrine carbonate reservoirs and includes internal subdivision marked by the Intra-Alagoas Unconformity.

Bivalve is a mollusk that possesses a shell composed of two hinged valves and, in the Brazilian Pre-Salt, commonly forms the dominant bioclastic fraction of coquina grainstones and rudstones. Its shells occur as articulated or, more commonly, disarticulated bioclasts with variable fragmentation, abrasion, and dissolution, and their abundance and taxonomic composition help interpret lacustrine depositional environments and hydrodynamic zones.

Microbial mat is a benthic, vertically layered, self-sustaining microbial community that develops at the liquid-solid interface of an environment. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it is commonly preserved as laminated or spongy carbonate fabric composed of microcrystalline filamentous calcitic laminae, locally with irregular porous cavities, and is associated with facies such as foam rock and microbial interlaminations.

Lamination is a primary sedimentary structure that consists of very thin, millimeter- to centimeter-scale layers in carbonate rock, typically arranged parallel to subparallel to bedding and varying from planar to wavy. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, laminations are commonly horizontal to sub-horizontal, may be regular, irregular, continuous, discontinuous, or crenulated, and reflect fine-scale depositional variation in alkaline to saline lacustrine settings.

Subsidence is a tectono-stratigraphic process that causes downward movement of the basin floor, thereby creating accommodation space for sediment accumulation. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it is commonly quantified as a subsidence rate through time from seismic-horizon thickness or back-stripping data, and its spatial and temporal variations control water depth, sediment thickness, and facies distribution between paleo-highs and basin areas.

Seismic facies is a seismostratigraphic unit that comprises a group of reflectors with characteristic amplitude, continuity, geometry, and frequency patterns that distinguish it from adjacent seismic units and can be related to architectural elements, depositional systems, or sedimentary environments. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates, seismic facies are defined by integrating seismic attributes with well information and are mapped as patterns such as tabular, mound, bank, fill, or parallel to infer reservoir boundaries, compartmentalization, and relative reservoir quality.

Microcrystalline calcite is a calcite aggregate that is composed of crystals so fine that individual grains are barely resolvable in thin section. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates, it commonly forms clots, peloids, microbial laminae, and spherulite nuclei, and it may also occur as a replacement product of Mg-clay-rich or fine siliciclastic matrices.

Lower Barra Velha Formation is the lower lithostratigraphic subdivision of the Barra Velha Formation that lies beneath the Intra-Alagoas Unconformity and is distinguished by Mg-rich clays, micrites, reworked facies, and locally basaltic intervals. In the Santos Basin pre-salt, it commonly records syn-tectonic deposition near faults and is generally more heterogeneous and less reservoir-prone than the overlying grainstone- and shrub-rich upper Barra Velha interval.

Diagenetic process is a geological alteration process that modifies a sediment or rock during and after deposition through fluid-mediated dissolution, cementation, recrystallization, replacement, or related mineral transformations. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates, it commonly includes dissolution of Mg-clays and carbonate fabrics, calcite, dolomite, or silica cementation, dolomitization, and silicification, which strongly control secondary porosity, permeability, and overall reservoir quality.
