Upper Barra Velha Formation is the upper stratigraphic unit of the Aptian Barra Velha Formation that overlies older pre-salt sedimentary packages and is characterized mainly by shrub-rich carbonates and grainstones in the Santos Basin. It commonly includes laminated limestones, dolostones, intraclastic grainstones or rudstones, and spherulitic to Mg-rich clayey facies deposited in a shallow alkaline lacustrine setting, and it forms one of the main reservoir intervals of the Brazilian Pre-Salt.

Fault zone is a structural deformation domain that encompasses the fault core and damage zone where fault displacement produces localized strain, intense shearing, fracturing, brecciation, and fault-rock development. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates, fault zones commonly connect matrix and fracture permeability and act as major conduits for vertical and lateral hydrothermal fluid circulation. They therefore strongly control dissolution porosity, karstification, and reservoir porosity-permeability distribution.

Alkalinity is a geochemical property of water or sediment pore fluid that expresses its capacity to neutralize acid through dissolved bases, mainly bicarbonate, carbonate, and hydroxide ions. In the Brazilian pre-salt lacustrine systems, elevated to hyper-alkaline conditions promoted shallow carbonate mineralization and the formation of Mg-clays, spherulites, and shrubstones, while commonly inhibiting metazoan life.

Barite is a sulfate mineral that consists of barium sulfate (BaSO4) and commonly precipitates as a late diagenetic to hydrothermal phase in Aptian pre-salt carbonates. In the Santos Basin, it typically occurs in minor amounts as prismatic crystals filling fractures in calcilutite or associated with tabular silicification, making it a useful indicator of post-depositional fluid circulation and hydrothermal alteration.

Hanging wall is the block of rock above a fault surface that, in extensional pre-salt settings, commonly subsides relative to the footwall along normal faults. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, the hanging wall commonly hosts growth wedges, syn-rift thickening, and hanging-wall folds generated by fault displacement variations, segment linkage, or later tectonic inversion.

Burial diagenesis is a post-depositional diagenetic process that alters carbonate sediments and rocks during progressive burial under increasing temperature, pressure, and evolving pore-fluid chemistry. In Brazilian pre-salt reservoirs, it commonly includes dissolution, cementation, recrystallization, dolomitization, and fracture filling during continued loading, and its interaction with deep or fault-related fluids can strongly modify porosity, permeability, and reservoir quality.

Rift basin is a sedimentary basin that forms by lithospheric extension and fault-controlled subsidence during continental or marine rifting. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it records the early basin stage linked to Gondwana breakup and typically comprises pre-rift, syn-rift, and post-rift successions, with syn-rift growth strata generated by active normal faulting and post-rift tabular strata deposited during thermal subsidence.

Halokinesis is a salt-tectonic deformation process that involves the flow and redistribution of evaporite layers under differential loading, generating structures such as diapirs, canopies, and salt windows. In the Santos Basin pre-salt system, it is a major control on basin restructuring and the structural styles of petroleum systems, influencing trap geometry, seal configuration, and hydrocarbon migration pathways through or around the salt section.

Mero Field is a giant pre-salt oil field that is located in the Santos Basin offshore southeastern Brazil and contains hydrocarbons in carbonate reservoirs within a large structural closure beneath the salt. Discovered in 2010 in the former Libra Block, it is one of Brazil's largest recent pre-salt discoveries, with estimated original oil in place of about 11.94 billion BOE and heterogeneous microbial carbonate and coquina reservoir facies.

Igneous rock is a rock type that forms by the cooling and solidification of magma or lava. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it occurs as Barremian–Aptian extrusive tholeiitic basalts and Santonian–Campanian alkaline intrusive bodies, commonly sills or saucer-shaped bodies, which may cut or follow the stratigraphy, show high seismic velocities, and strongly influence reservoir volume, flow behavior, pressure support, and associated diagenetic alteration.

Calcirudite is a coarse-grained clastic carbonate rock that is composed mainly of granule- to pebble-sized intra- or extra-clasts, chiefly fragments of limestone and dolostone, in reworked or hybrid carbonate successions. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly occurs as a massive, poorly sorted ruditic facies dominated by carbonate intraclasts, and it may be either clast-supported or matrix-supported with minor chert, silica, silicate grains, or ooidal-peloidal components.

Mechanical compaction is a diagenetic process that reduces sediment volume and primary porosity by physically rearranging, tightening, and slightly deforming grains and laminae under burial stress, without substantial pressure-solution or other chemical mass transfer. In Brazilian pre-salt lacustrine carbonates, it is typically recognized by tight grain packing, crinkled argillaceous laminae, concave-convex to long grain contacts, and minor grain deformation, and it commonly postdates some early dolomite cements.

Hydrothermal vent is a pipe-like geological complex that forms by the fracturing, transport, and eruption of deep-sourced hydrothermal fluids and sediments, commonly in association with intrusive or volcanic activity. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, these vents can strongly influence lacustrine carbonate systems by modifying water alkalinity and mineral supply, promoting travertine and shrub/spherulite development, and locally enhancing dissolution, vuggy porosity, and reservoir fluid flow.

Magnesian clay is a syngenetic Mg-rich clay-mineral aggregate that is composed mainly of stevensite and kerolite and occurs in Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates as massive to laminated deposits commonly associated with calcitic spherulites. In Brazilian Pre-Salt reservoirs, these aggregates are chemically unstable and are commonly deformed by spherulite growth and overprinted by dolomitization, silicification, or dissolution, sometimes together with detrital siliciclastic material.

Dolomudstone is a mud-supported dolomitic carbonate rock that is composed mainly of very fine dolomite crystals with variable mud content and, in some cases, interlayered fine calcite particles arranged in irregular discontinuous laminations. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, laminated dolomudstone commonly occurs as thin beds and generally acts as a non-reservoir because its porosity is very low and dominated by tiny intercrystalline and interparticle pores. Where intense fracturing is present, however, it may locally develop significant fracture-related porosity and permeability.

Bioclastic rudstone is a coarse-grained bioclastic carbonate rock that contains skeletal grains larger than 2 mm, commonly dominated in the Brazilian Pre-Salt by fragmented and disarticulated bivalve shells with variable sorting and common intraclasts. In Pre-Salt lacustrine reservoirs, it commonly shows a highly heterogeneous pore system with interparticle, moldic, intraparticle, and vugular porosity, so its permeability varies strongly with pore type and diagenetic overprint such as dissolution, recrystallization, and cementation.

Cyclothem is a meter-scale stratigraphic succession that records a repeated lacustrine shallowing-upward evaporitic cycle from flooding-phase laminated carbonate muds to spherulitic and shrub-like calcite facies, commonly capped by thin grainstones of reworked shrub, spherulite, and intraclast debris. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, especially in the Barra Velha and equivalent units, cyclothems are typically about 0.75–5 m thick and reflect alternations between flooding, evaporation, and changes in pH, alkalinity, and Mg-silicate precipitation in shallow alkaline lakes.

Heterogeneity is a reservoir characteristic that consists of spatial variations in rock, petrophysical, and flow properties produced by depositional, structural, and diagenetic processes. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates, it occurs across multiple scales, commonly as cyclic alternations of high- and low-quality layers and contrasting pore systems, and it can create flow baffles or sealed compartments that control reservoir connectivity and production behavior.

Bioclast is a sedimentary carbonate grain that consists of whole or fragmented skeletal remains of organisms, commonly bivalves, ostracods, and gastropods in Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates. In bioclastic grainstones, rudstones, and coquinas, bioclasts commonly occur as reworked or abraded shell material and may be micritized, recrystallized, dolomitized, or silicified, influencing interparticle and intraparticle porosity.

Intraclastic rudstone is a grain-supported carbonate rock that is dominated by reworked intraclasts larger than 2 mm, commonly derived from crystal shrub crusts, spherulitestones, laminated carbonates, dolomudstones, and other lacustrine carbonate fragments. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it typically shows poor to moderate sorting, variable grain rounding, and may include silicified particles or minor clay matrix. It commonly preserves interparticle porosity and may develop additional secondary porosity through dissolution.

Lake level is a depositional boundary condition that defines the elevation of the lacustrine water surface relative to a reference datum and controls bathymetry, accommodation space, and facies distribution in Pre-Salt carbonate systems. In forward stratigraphic modeling, it is commonly represented as a relative or absolute variation curve derived and calibrated from lithology logs, seismic data, and conceptual depositional models to reproduce deepening and shallowing trends through time.

Lacustrine system is a depositional system that develops within a lake basin and controls the sedimentary, chemical, and ecological processes that generate lake deposits. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it refers to the vast Aptian alkaline, stratified to meromictic lake system that occupied much of the South Atlantic rift depression, hosted carbonate accumulation, and preceded the deposition of the overlying evaporites.

Spherulitic mudstone is a mud-rich lacustrine carbonate facies that consists of a mud matrix containing dispersed spherulites in amounts below 70%. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it is commonly parallel laminated, with rounded spherulitic grains that are loosely packed and rarely in contact. Compared with Mg-rich mudstone, it typically shows higher porosity and permeability and a predominant free-fluid signature.

Silica nodule is a diagenetic siliceous concretion that occurs as a discrete almond-shaped to rounded body of microcrystalline to macrocrystalline quartz within pre-salt lacustrine carbonate mudstones and dolomudstones. In the Santos Basin, it commonly forms during early diagenesis together with silica layers, reflecting localized silica precipitation driven by changes in pore-water chemistry and possibly by dissolution of Mg-clay minerals.

Wave base is a hydrodynamic depth threshold that marks the effective lower limit of significant wave-induced energy and sediment reworking on the substrate. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates, it is commonly treated as a shallow boundary, around 10 m in stratigraphic models, that helps distinguish wave-agitated shrubstone and reworked facies near or above it from lower-energy fine-grained or chemogenic deposits below it.

Rifting is a tectonic process that stretches and thins continental lithosphere, producing block faulting, subsidence, and fault-bounded basin development during continental breakup. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, the rifting phase was accompanied by extensive volcanism and generated half-grabens and structural relief that controlled paleophysiography, lacustrine chemistry, and the distribution of syn-rift sediments and reservoir facies.

Effective porosity is a petrophysical property that quantifies the interconnected portion of a rock's pore volume available for fluid storage and flow, excluding isolated pores and non-contributing bound water. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates, it is commonly estimated from NMR logs and interpreted together with total porosity, free-fluid content, permeability, and fracture intensity to assess reservoir quality and production behavior.

Sepiolite is a hydrated magnesium silicate clay mineral that occurs as a minor authigenic Mg-silicate phase in Aptian pre-salt lacustrine carbonates, commonly associated with kerolite and stevensite in clay-rich substrates. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it is typically subordinate in abundance and may reflect alteration of stevensitic clays, including under exposure-related or evaporative conditions.

Replacement is a diagenetic process that substitutes a pre-existing mineral or sedimentary component with a new mineral in situ, commonly through coupled dissolution and precipitation and often with preservation of the original texture or morphology. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates, replacement commonly affects spherulites, stevensitic clays, fine grains, and growth-framework elements by silica, dolomite, or calcite, and it can create microporosity or vugular porosity while strongly modifying reservoir quality.

Outer High is an uplifted basement structural high that forms a broad NE-SW-trending elevated zone in the Santos Basin and controls pre-salt depositional architecture by creating a shallow, clastic-starved structural ramp favorable to carbonate and evaporite accumulation. In the Barra Velha interval, it was established before deposition, includes major culminations such as the Sugar Loaf High and Tupi High, and is closely associated with prolific reservoir development and giant oil fields.

Basement high is a fault-bounded structural high that forms a topographic elevation of the basement above adjacent basement lows. In the Brazilian pre-salt, such highs commonly control accommodation and depositional architecture by focusing onlap and aggradation of lacustrine carbonate platforms, and they are typically associated with thinner or locally eroded pre-salt intervals relative to neighboring lows.

Reservoir rock is a sedimentary rock or rock facies that has sufficient porosity and permeability to store hydrocarbons and allow their flow through the subsurface reservoir. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, reservoir rocks are chiefly lacustrine carbonates of the Itapema and Barra Velha formations, especially bioclastic limestones or coquinas and shrub-dominated facies, whose quality is highly heterogeneous and strongly controlled by depositional texture and diagenetic processes such as dissolution, neomorphism, silicification, dolomitization, and mineral replacement.

An alkaline lacustrine environment is a lake depositional setting that has high-pH, commonly saline waters enriched in dissolved Mg, Ca, Si, Cl, and HCO3, favoring chemical precipitation of carbonate and related minerals. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, these conditions commonly generated magnesian clays, calcite spherulites, shrubs, laminites, and stromatolitic facies in the water column and at or just below the lake floor, while also limiting normal molluscan faunas.

Carnallite is a hydrous potassium-magnesium chloride evaporite mineral (KMgCl3·6H2O) that precipitates from highly concentrated brines and forms part of the more soluble salt assemblage of the Ariri Formation. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly occurs associated with halite, anhydrite, tachyhydrite, and sylvite, recording late-stage evaporitic concentration under arid and restricted basin conditions.

Crystalline basement is a pre-sedimentary bedrock unit that consists of consolidated igneous and metamorphic rocks underlying the pre-salt succession, typically Precambrian granites, gneisses, and related metasediments in the Santos and Campos basins. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly forms the rift footwall and a fractured host rock for fluid flow and diagenesis, locally showing brecciation and veins filled by quartz, pyrite, and Fe-rich dolomite-ankerite.

Camboriú Formation is a syn-rift volcanic stratigraphic unit that records the onset of rifting in the Santos Basin and forms the economic basement of the Brazilian pre-salt succession. It is composed predominantly of basaltic rocks, including basaltic dyke swarms, and its top is commonly recognized in seismic data as a strong positive reflector overlain by the Piçarras Formation.

Spherulitic shrubstone is an in-situ lacustrine carbonate facies that is dominated by shrubs, contains a subordinate spherulitic component, and includes less than 10% mud. In the Barra Velha Formation it typically comprises medium- to coarse-sized shrubs with very fine- to coarse-grained spherulites between or on top of shrub branches, and it may show fining-upward to smaller shrubs or spherulites. It commonly has calcite, dolomite, and locally silica cement and develops mainly fabric-selective inter-branch porosity plus intra-shrub dissolution porosity.

Chemical precipitation is a depositional process that directly forms carbonate or related minerals from chemically supersaturated lake water without detrital transport. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly took place in alkaline lacustrine settings, where changes in Mg/Ca ratio, dissolved silica, and microbial influence promoted the precipitation of hydrated Mg-silicate gels, low-Mg calcite or aragonite, and fabrics such as spherulites, shrubs, and oncolitic carbonate deposits.

Gneiss is a foliated metamorphic rock that displays coarse-grained compositional banding produced by high-grade recrystallization of pre-existing rocks. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt context, it commonly forms part of the crystalline basement and may also occur as clasts in synrift to sag conglomerates, indicating erosion of uplifted metamorphic source terrains.

Fracture porosity is a non-matrix porosity type that consists of void space within natural open fractures and microfractures cutting the carbonate rock. In Brazilian Pre-Salt reservoirs, it may result from primary or diagenetic fracturing, is commonly concentrated in fault-related fractured zones, and mainly contributes to reservoir connectivity and permeability rather than matrix storage.

Florianopolis High is a dominantly magmatic structural high that forms the southern boundary of the Santos Basin and separates it from the Pelotas Basin. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt context, it acted as a basin-scale physiographic barrier that helped isolate the Santos Basin from fully marine waters to the south, influencing its tectono-sedimentary evolution and lacustrine carbonate development.

Rift supersequence is a tectonostratigraphic supersequence that records the syn-rift phase of basin evolution under lithospheric extension and fault-controlled subsidence. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it typically comprises continental siliciclastic and volcanic deposits together with lacustrine coquinas, organic-rich shales, and locally ooid-bearing facies, such as those of the Piçarras and Itapema formations or the basal Lagoa Feia Group, deposited mainly from the Barremian to Lower Aptian in half-graben depocenters.

Eoaptian is an informal chronostratigraphic interval that corresponds to the earliest part of the Aptian Stage in the Early Cretaceous. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it commonly denotes the time of syn-rift Itapema Formation deposition, including lacustrine coquinas and related carbonates, broadly around 126 to 123 Ma in the cited stratigraphic framework.

Sedimentary facies is a mappable body of sediment or sedimentary rock that is distinguished by a characteristic combination of lithology, texture, sedimentary structures, and vertical or lateral association, reflecting a specific depositional environment or process. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, sedimentary facies are identified by integrating core, thin-section, well-log, and seismic data to reconstruct lacustrine settings such as profundal, slope, bench interior, and bench margin, and to distinguish in-situ from reworked carbonate deposits.

Gondwana supercontinent is a supercontinent that amalgamated South America, Africa, and other southern continental blocks before its breakup initiated the South Atlantic rifting that shaped the Brazilian pre-salt basins. In the Santos Basin context, its Early Cretaceous rupture involved lithospheric stretching and locally hotspot-related thermal anomalies, producing crustal thinning and the rift to post-rift evolution that hosts the pre-salt section.

Sapinhoá Field is an offshore pre-salt oil field that is located in the Santos Basin, Brazil, and contains Aptian carbonate reservoirs mainly within the Barra Velha Formation beneath the salt section. In the context of Brazilian pre-salt geology, it is a key reservoir area for studying facies architecture, porosity distribution, and diagenetic controls in lacustrine carbonates, including intervals near the base of the Ariri Formation.

Calcarenite is a clastic carbonate rock that is composed predominantly of sand-sized carbonate grains or intraclasts, typically representing reworked carbonate sediment and, in hybrid varieties, containing less than 50% siliciclastic material. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly consists of ooids and intra- or extra-clasts of limestone or dolostone, with subordinate silica or chert and minor silicate grains, and may occur as laminated resedimented beds with interparticle and intraparticle porosity.

Passive margin is a continental-margin tectonic setting that develops after continental rifting and breakup, when oceanic crust is established and the basin enters a post-rift drift stage dominated mainly by subsidence rather than active plate-boundary deformation. In the Brazilian South Atlantic basins, this phase corresponds to the free-marine post-salt evolution, including Albian shallow-water carbonate platform deposition later overlain by more siliciclastic successions, and the Santos, Campos, and Espírito Santo basins are typical magma-poor passive margins.

Bivalve rudstone is a bioclastic carbonate rudstone that consists predominantly of coarse bivalve shell bioclasts, commonly disarticulated, fragmented, and variably reworked. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly forms a coquina reservoir facies with massive, poorly to well sorted, chaotic to subparallel fabric, and may preserve interparticle, intraparticle, moldic, and locally vuggy porosity despite diagenetic alteration such as dissolution, neomorphism, calcite cementation, dolomitization, or silicification.

Stylolite is a pressure-solution seam that forms by localized dissolution during compaction and concentrates insoluble or less soluble minerals along an irregular surface in carbonate rocks. In Brazilian pre-salt reservoirs, stylolites commonly occur in bioclastic rudstones, hybrid facies, cherts, and chert-dolostone contacts, where they are enriched in illite and other residual minerals, may truncate earlier cements, and can be associated with symmetric porosity enhancement.

Vugular porosity is a secondary pore type that consists of dissolution-generated cavities larger than the particles composing the carbonate rock. In Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates, it is widespread across several facies, but where vugs dominate the pore system permeability is commonly low because pore connectivity is poor, whereas association with interparticle porosity can improve reservoir quality.

Microbial laminite is a laminated microbialite that is formed by the growth and lithification of benthic microbial mats, producing fine carbonate-rich laminae. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly occurs as finely crinkly to wavy laminated carbonate mudstone interpreted as lithified microbial mats in shallow lacustrine to supralittoral–eulittoral settings, and it may be overprinted by calcite, dolomite, or silica replacement during diagenesis.

Regional seal is a basin-scale sealing unit that laterally extends over reservoir rocks and prevents the upward migration and leakage of hydrocarbons. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, the regional seal is formed mainly by the evaporites of the Ariri Formation, especially halite and anhydrite, which overlie the Barra Velha and related reservoirs and provide an effective seal despite large thickness variations.

Sag stage is a tectono-stratigraphic stage that records the broad subsidence and relative tectonic quiescence between active rifting and passive-margin drift, commonly with localized fault reactivation and a transition from continental/lacustrine to shallow-marine conditions. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it begins above the pre-Alagoas unconformity and includes the Barra Velha lacustrine carbonates and shales, followed by the thick evaporites of the Ariri Formation.

Calcite shrub is a calcitic growth fabric that consists of branching to fan-shaped aggregates of radiating fibrous to coarse bladed fascicular-optic calcite crystals, giving a shrub-like external morphology. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly occurs as in-situ horizontal layers or low domal crusts in lacustrine carbonates of the Barra Velha Formation and is typically associated with rapid carbonate precipitation in shallow, highly saturated waters.

Reworked carbonate is a lacustrine carbonate lithofacies that is composed mainly of transported and redeposited clasts of calcitic spherulites and/or calcitic shrubs, typically occurring as grainstone- to rudstone-like calciarenites and calcirudites. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt Barra Velha Formation, it commonly contains grains from fine sand to pebble size, shows moderate sorting and massive to cross-stratified textures, and may include peloids, ostracod bioclasts, Mg-rich clays, and minor detrital siliciclastics. Where siliciclastic content exceeds about 10%, it is distinguished as reworked carbonate with siliciclastic content (RC-si), and the facies commonly forms relatively high-quality reservoir intervals due to open-framework and locally enhanced secondary porosity.

Early diagenesis is a diagenetic stage that modifies sediments during or immediately after deposition at the water-sediment interface or under very shallow burial, before deeper burial alteration begins. In Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates, it commonly involves dissolution of primary Mg-clays and some carbonate fabrics, recrystallization of shrubs and spherulites, and precipitation of early calcite, dolomite, and silica cements. These processes may generate vuggy and moldic porosity, but they also commonly coat or fill pores and reduce pore size and connectivity.

Continental margin is a tectonostratigraphic transition zone that links continental crust to the adjacent oceanic basin and organizes the structural and stratigraphic framework of offshore basins. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, the architecture and relative position of the continental margin strongly influence rift-to-sag evolution, fault displacement, salt thickness and mobilization, and consequently reservoir distribution, compartmentalization, and fluid migration.

Marine incursion is a hydrologic event that introduces seawater into a previously isolated or restricted basin. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it refers mainly to late Aptian marine ingress into the post-rift lacustrine system, which increased salinity, promoted evaporite deposition such as the Ariri Formation, and marked the transition toward shallow marine conditions.

Downlap is a seismic reflector termination that occurs where inclined or progradational strata terminate downdip against a lower-lying surface. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it is used in seismic stratigraphic interpretation to identify progradational stacking patterns, define stratigraphic boundaries, and infer changes in accommodation and depositional architecture; in tectonically rotated settings, original downlap may locally appear as apparent onlap.

Pore throat is a constricted opening in a porous rock that connects adjacent pore bodies and strongly controls capillary entry, fluid flow, and permeability. In Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates, pore throat size is commonly quantified by mercury injection capillary pressure (MICP) and classified as micro when less than 0.5 µm, meso between 0.5 and 5 µm, and macro when greater than 5 µm. Larger pore throats generally indicate better reservoir quality because they allow easier fluid movement through the pore network.

Mud is a fine-grained sediment that occurs in Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates as matrix between grains and as laminated or massive beds, and is composed of variable proportions of clay minerals, calcite, dolomite, and silica. In the Barra Velha Formation, it commonly forms millimetric to centimetric plane-parallel to slightly wavy laminae, with microcrystalline calcite in lighter layers and dolomite, organic matter, Mg-clays, and locally silica in darker layers. Clay-rich and carbonate-mud components may also be partially replaced by microcrystalline dolomite and silica.

Hydrocarbon is an organic chemical compound that consists exclusively of carbon and hydrogen atoms. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt context, hydrocarbons occur mainly as crude oil and natural gas generated from source rocks and accumulated within porous, vuggy, and fractured lacustrine carbonate reservoirs beneath the salt layer.

Lacustrine carbonate platform is a carbonate depositional system that develops in lake settings on broad structural highs and accumulates shallow-water carbonate sediments during sag-stage basin evolution. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly forms large seismically mappable bodies composed of microbialites and bioclastic limestones, including shrubby boundstones and spherulite-intraclast grainstones that constitute key reservoir facies, while muddier wackestones and packstones tend to increase toward platform margins.

Siltstone is a siliciclastic sedimentary rock that is composed predominantly of silt-sized particles, with a higher proportion of silt and less clay than mudstone. In the Brazilian pre-salt Barra Velha succession, it commonly occurs as massive or incipiently plane-parallel laminated microfacies, ranging from coarse to fine silt and locally containing trace very fine to fine sand. Its main constituents are typically K-feldspar, monocrystalline quartz, white mica, and clay minerals.

Mechanical subsidence is a tectonic subsidence process that is driven by crustal and lithospheric stretching during the rift phase, creating accommodation space and commonly producing normal faulting, half-grabens, and basement-fault reactivation. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it defines the syn-rift stage that preceded regional thermal subsidence of the sag phase and strongly controlled lacustrine paleogeography and facies distribution.

Gastropod is a mollusk that typically bears a single, commonly coiled shell and whose skeletal remains occur as bioclasts in Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonate rocks. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, gastropod shells are usually minor, little-abraded components of coquinas associated with bivalves and oncoids. Their occurrence can reflect variations in salinity and hydrodynamic energy and may preserve intraparticle porosity.

Intergranular porosity is a porosity type that comprises void space between adjacent grains, shell fragments, or other sedimentary particles in a rock. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonate reservoirs, especially grainstones and packstones, it commonly forms the dominant reservoir pore system and can support good storage and permeability where preserved or enlarged, although it may be reduced by intergranular micrite or by calcite and quartz cementation.

Mg-silicate clay is a magnesium-rich layer silicate clay mineral that forms syngenetically in the alkaline, saline lacustrine carbonates of the Brazilian Pre-Salt, mainly as stevensite and kerolite. In these reservoirs it commonly constitutes the matrix of Mg-claystone and spherulitic facies, and its later dissolution or replacement by carbonate or silica is a major control on porosity evolution and silicification.

Depositional system is a sedimentary system that comprises the genetically related environments, facies, and processes through which sediment is produced, transported, and accumulated in a basin. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly denotes the lacustrine carbonate framework whose facies distribution, depositional cycles, and sedimentation rates are controlled by lake palaeotopography, tectonism, climate, water chemistry, and fault-related transfer zones, thereby governing reservoir architecture and heterogeneity.

Marine environment is a depositional setting that is characterized by the persistent influence of seawater and marine circulation, from shallow coastal to open-marine conditions. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt context, it denotes the stage when restricted lacustrine systems gave way to marine ingress and ultimately to open South Atlantic conditions, preceding or accompanying evaporite deposition above the main carbonate reservoirs.

Evaporite deposit is a sedimentary deposit that consists of minerals precipitated and accumulated from highly evaporative saline waters, typically including halite and anhydrite in restricted lacustrine to shallow marine settings. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, Aptian evaporite deposits such as those of the Ariri and Retiro formations may also contain sylvite and carnallite, and they form the regional stratigraphic seal over the underlying carbonate reservoirs.

Carbonate facies is a sedimentary facies that is defined by a distinctive set of carbonate textures, fabrics, components, and structures formed under particular depositional conditions. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it is used to distinguish facies such as laminites, grainstones, stromatolites or shrubs, and spherulitites, as well as autochthonous or in-situ versus allochthonous or reworked carbonates, because their vertical and lateral distribution governs reservoir architecture and quality.

Guarujá Formation is a post-salt Albian stratigraphic formation that comprises the basal marine carbonate interval of the early drift megasequence in the Santos Basin, overlying the evaporites. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt it is typically a thin carbonate package, commonly 10 to 30 m thick, dominated by fine-grained mudstones and calcilutites deposited in distal restricted marine settings, with local shallow-platform oolitic and bioclastic facies.

Lacustrine coquina is a bioclastic carbonate rock that consists predominantly of accumulated and commonly fragmented mollusk shells deposited in a lacustrine environment. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly formed in the Itapema Formation on structural highs under shallow, high-energy rift-lake conditions, occurring as coquina banks and related bar, beach, washover, and tempestite deposits interbedded with shales.

São Paulo Plateau is a regional structural high in the eastern Santos Basin that comprises a set of basement highs, including the Outer High, defined by the base-evaporite unconformity and expressed as elevated Aptian palaeotopography. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it is the main exploration province where these distal, clastic-starved highs provided the topographic template for accumulation of Barra Velha lacustrine carbonates. It is also interpreted to be linked to failed northward propagation of seafloor spreading near the Florianópolis Fracture Zone.

Itanhaém Formation is a lithostratigraphic unit in the Santos Basin that records deeper-water sedimentation after the drowning of the shallow-marine carbonate platform of the Guarujá Formation during the early drift stage. In the regional stratigraphic framework, it marks the transition from platform carbonate deposition to more distal marine conditions above the pre-salt succession.

High-energy environment is a depositional setting that is subject to strong hydrodynamic forces, such as waves, currents, or sheetfloods, which promote sediment transport, reworking, winnowing, and erosion. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates, it commonly refers to shallow platform or marginal lake areas above or near wave base, where reworked carbonates, intraclasts, fragmented bioclasts, and poor preservation of delicate primary phases are typical.

Campanian is a Late Cretaceous geologic age that spans approximately 83 to 72 million years ago and, in the Brazilian Pre-Salt context, represents the initial interval of the Campanian–Maastrichtian tectono-diagenetic event identified from replacive and vein-filling carbonate cements. Although the main Pre-Salt reservoirs are Aptian in age, the Campanian is important because it marks a later phase of burial-related diagenesis that affected mineral assemblages, precipitation temperatures, and burial conditions in the Northern Campos Basin.

Lake-level fluctuation is a relative water-level variation that changes lake elevation through time, thereby modifying bathymetry and accommodation in lacustrine carbonate systems. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it is a key control on water depth, energy conditions, shoreline position, and the lateral and vertical shifting of facies and hiatuses that form depositional cycles. Repeated rises and falls may also expose carbonate deposits to penecontemporaneous karstification, locally creating or enhancing reservoir porosity.

Mesodiagenesis is a burial diagenetic stage that modifies pre-salt carbonate rocks after eodiagenesis through continued calcite dissolution, recrystallization of the primary carbonate fabric, coarse pore-filling cementation, late fracturing, and solid bitumen emplacement. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly generates secondary intragranular and vuggy porosity by dissolution and fracturing, while macrocrystalline dolomite, quartz, and subordinate mineral cements may partially to completely occlude that porosity.

Talc is a magnesium-rich phyllosilicate mineral that precipitates in the Brazilian pre-salt under highly alkaline lacustrine conditions, commonly as hydrated talc formed from Mg-rich silica gel at about pH 9 to 10. In the Barra Velha Formation it is characterized by low crystallinity and a defective turbostratic structure, and its late diagenetic transformation releases silica and magnesium that favor the precipitation of silica and dolomite.

Magmatism is a geological process that involves the generation, ascent, emplacement, and possible eruption of magma within and above the crust. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it includes intrusive and extrusive events from rift to drift stages that are commonly linked to tectonic controls and may accompany hydrothermal alteration, although their thermal influence on carbonate reservoir diagenesis can be locally limited and is not always the main controlling factor.

Oil-water contact is a reservoir fluid boundary that marks the depth at which the oil-saturated interval passes into the underlying water-saturated interval. In Brazilian pre-salt carbonate reservoirs, it is commonly estimated from a significant resistivity-log contrast, calibrated with porosity logs and pressure data, and spatial irregularities in its depth may indicate perched water effects or reservoir compartmentalization.

Rifted margin is a continental margin that develops through lithospheric extension, faulting, and crustal thinning, commonly culminating in plate rupture and the onset of oceanic spreading. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt basins, it is expressed by fault-compartmentalized crustal blocks and syn-rift stratigraphic sequences bounded by key unconformities from rift onset to breakup, followed by increased thermal subsidence.

Upper Aptian is a chronostratigraphic subdivision that represents the later part of the Aptian Stage of the Lower Cretaceous, corresponding in the Brazilian pre-salt to the upper pre-salt interval deposited immediately before widespread salt accumulation. In the cited Campos Basin framework, it is the interval bounded below by the mid-Aptian unconformity and above by the late Aptian base-salt surface. In pre-salt reservoir studies, it commonly encompasses sag-phase carbonate deposition, including the upper-sag succession of the Barra Velha Formation, which is associated with progradational shallowing-upward cycles and favorable porosity-permeability development.

Aquifer is a subsurface hydrogeologic unit that stores and transmits groundwater through permeable or fractured rocks, including confined systems beneath the pre-salt succession and regional flow paths in fractured crystalline basement. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, aquifers can recharge lacustrine systems and provide regional pressure support to reservoirs during production, but they may also drive water influx, water coning, and early water breakthrough.

Rhombohedral dolomite is a diagenetic dolomite crystal fabric that consists of rhomb-shaped dolomite crystals occurring within carbonate rocks, commonly in interstitial spaces among spherulites, calcite shrubs, and fascicular calcite crusts. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt Barra Velha Formation, it is the most common dolomite type and is most abundant in spherulite-rich facies, with many occurrences formed before mechanical compaction and some compositions approaching stoichiometric burial dolomite.

Carbonate precipitation is a geochemical process that forms carbonate minerals from solution when water becomes supersaturated under specific physicochemical conditions. In the continental carbonate systems relevant to the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it occurs only under particular lake or spring chemistries and is commonly favored by factors such as CO2 degassing, evaporation, and pH buffering rather than by temperature alone. Its expression is strongly controlled by the geomorphological, geochemical, and hydrologic setting, and may be locally influenced by microbial activity.

Oncoid is a coated carbonate grain that consists of a nucleus surrounded by irregular to concentric microbial laminae produced by cyanobacterial accretion, commonly while the particle is intermittently rolled in very shallow lacustrine water. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, oncoids occur as dominant allochems in oncoidal grainstones, rudstones, and packstones/floatstones, where they are typically spherical to semi-spherical and may preserve or develop intraparticle dissolution porosity.

Floatstone is a matrix-supported carbonate rock that contains granule- to pebble-size clasts floating within a finer-grained matrix. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, especially in the Barra Velha Formation, it commonly corresponds to matrix-supported calcirudite with angular fragments of microbialite, tufa, shrubstone, chert, and other carbonate lithologies in a dark sand-silty matrix, typically indicating reworked or debris-flow deposition.

Mg-clay is a magnesium-rich clay mineral assemblage that forms part of the matrix of Brazilian pre-salt carbonate facies, commonly in association with calcite spherulites and dolomite. In the Santos Basin it consists mainly of Mg-smectitic clays, with rare sepiolite, and its dissolution or replacement by calcite can generate secondary porosity even though Mg-clay-rich facies are initially of low reservoir quality.

Pre-salt play is a hydrocarbon play that comprises Lower Cretaceous lacustrine carbonate reservoirs beneath a thick Aptian salt seal, charged by prolific lacustrine source rocks. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it typically includes coquina and microbialite reservoirs in syn-rift to sag successions, commonly draped over structural highs, with vertical faults aiding migration and strong lateral heterogeneity in reservoir quality representing a major risk.

Atapu Field is an offshore pre-salt oil field that lies in the central Santos Basin, about 200 km off the Brazilian coast in water depths of 2,000 to 2,300 m, and contains giant carbonate reservoirs beneath the salt layer. It is part of the Iara Complex together with the Berbigão and Sururu fields, has estimated oil volumes of 2.5 to 4 billion barrels of oil equivalent, and ranks among Brazil's major pre-salt producing fields.

Guaratiba Group is a Lower Cretaceous lithostratigraphic group of the Santos Basin that records the rift to post-rift evolution of the Brazilian pre-salt, comprising the Camboriú, Piçarras, Itapema, Barra Velha, and Ariri formations. Deposited from roughly the Hauterivian to the Aptian in continental lacustrine to evaporitic settings, it contains the main pre-salt carbonate reservoirs, especially the Itapema and Barra Velha formations.

Neomorphism is a diagenetic process that recrystallizes original carbonate constituents, commonly aragonitic bioclasts, into new crystal forms in situ. In Brazilian Pre-Salt bioclastic grainstones and rudstones, it commonly affects bivalve and gastropod shells and competes with dissolution, with its predominance tending to preserve primary interparticle porosity and favor higher permeability.

Depositional facies is a sedimentary facies that records the original depositional conditions of a rock through its primary composition, texture, and fabric. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates, depositional facies include in-situ shrub- and spherulite-rich deposits as well as reworked carbonate facies ranging from mudstones to intraclastic grainstones and rudstones. They are distinguished from diagenetic facies, which may derive from similar original deposits but now display different fabrics because of post-depositional alteration.

Cabiúnas Formation is a volcanic lithostratigraphic unit that forms the basal pre-salt succession of the Campos Basin and is composed mainly of tholeiitic basalts and associated volcaniclastics linked to the onset of rifting. It underlies the Lagoa Feia Group and is often treated as part of the basement in structural studies. Reported K–Ar ages for its basalts are about 134–122 Ma, although some of the younger values may reflect alteration effects.

Itabapoana Formation is a lithostratigraphic unit of the Lagoa Feia Group that is composed predominantly of proximal marginal clastic sediments, including conglomerates, sandstones, siltstones, and red shales, deposited around Aptian lacustrine systems in the northern Campos Basin pre-salt succession. It commonly grades laterally into more lacustrine deposits such as those of the Gargaú Formation. In subsurface data, it may be difficult to distinguish from the Atafona Formation.

Retiro Formation is a post-rift evaporitic stratigraphic formation that records Aptian deposition in a highly evaporative shallow-marine setting following marine incursions under arid climatic conditions. It consists predominantly of anhydrite, halite, sylvite, and carnallite, may reach about 2000 m in thickness, and forms an important regional stratigraphic seal over Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonate reservoirs and major hydrocarbon accumulations.

Pre-salt section is a Lower Cretaceous stratigraphic interval that comprises the sedimentary succession deposited before salt emplacement in the South Atlantic basins, lying beneath the Aptian evaporites and including syn-rift to sag-stage deposits such as lacustrine carbonates of the Barra Velha Formation. In the Brazilian Santos and Campos basins, this interval contains giant hydrocarbon accumulations and is a key target for seismic, stratigraphic, and reservoir characterization studies because of its complex carbonate heterogeneity.

Matrix porosity is a component of rock porosity that resides within the carbonate rock matrix itself rather than in large karst-related vugs, mega- and giga-pores, or fractures. In Brazilian Pre-Salt reservoirs, it commonly constitutes a major part of effective porosity and can be identified in acoustic image logs by lower-amplitude matrix responses, whereas low-porosity matrix shows higher amplitudes.

Facies association is a sedimentological grouping of related facies that occur together in a characteristic vertical and/or lateral stacking pattern and collectively represent a specific depositional subenvironment or process regime. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly groups several carbonate facies into interpretable units such as back-barrier, foreshore-shoreface, bioclastic bar, tempestite, or offshore deposits, helping define depositional architecture and relative lake-level changes.

Water chemistry is the geochemical condition of a water body that is defined by parameters such as pH, alkalinity, redox state, temperature, pCO2, and dissolved ion activities, thereby controlling mineral saturation and biological development. In Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates, changes in lake-water chemistry driven by evaporation, climate, and magmatic or hydrothermal inputs govern the precipitation of magnesian clays, calcite, dolomite, and related microbial and faunal assemblages.

Marl is a fine-grained mixed sedimentary rock that contains substantial proportions of carbonate minerals and clay. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt context, it commonly refers to calcareous mud-rich lacustrine intervals interbedded with cleaner carbonate facies, typically indicating greater argillaceous input and lower reservoir quality than purer carbonates.

Santos Outer High is an intrabasinal structural high that comprises an uplifted, fault-bounded basement block system in the central Santos Basin, forming a NE-SW-trending closure and a long-lived palaeohigh during Barremian–Aptian pre-salt deposition. Its elevated and relatively clastic-starved setting favored the development of extensive lacustrine carbonates, especially in the Barra Velha interval, and it contains the principal oil fields of the Santos pre-salt province.

Florianópolis High is a regional structural and physiographic high that forms the southern boundary of the Santos Basin and separates it from the Pelotas Basin, being dominantly magmatic in origin. In the Brazilian pre-salt context, it acted as a paleogeographic barrier that helped isolate the Santos Basin from fully marine waters to the south, influencing its distinct tectono-sedimentary evolution and lacustrine carbonate reservoir development.

Evaporitic deposit is a chemical sedimentary deposit that forms by precipitation and accumulation of soluble salts from highly concentrated saline waters under strong evaporation. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly refers to the Aptian Ariri Formation evaporites—mainly halite and anhydrite, with locally potassium and magnesium salts—that overlie the Barra Velha carbonates, form a thick regional seal, and can undergo early salt movement because of internal rheological contrasts.

Reservoir facies is a depositional or diagenetic facies that has pore-system architecture and petrophysical properties favorable for hydrocarbon storage and flow. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, the best reservoir facies commonly include stromatolites, grainstones, and shrub- or spherulite-rich facies, where connected primary porosity may be further enhanced by dissolution and fractures. Distinguishing reservoir facies from tighter muddy, bench-interior, or profundal facies is fundamental for predicting porosity-permeability distribution and production behavior.

Lake margin is the boundary zone of a lacustrine system that marks the transition between the open lake and adjacent shallow-water or exposed areas, and whose position migrates with lake-level changes. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, distance to the lake margin is a key control on water depth, hydrodynamic energy, facies distribution, and reservoir heterogeneity, and its migration can be inferred from seismic onlap patterns.

Saponite is a magnesium-rich smectite clay mineral that belongs to the Mg-smectite group and occurs in Aptian Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates as part of the authigenic Mg-silicate clay assemblage. In Santos Basin reservoir facies, it is typically a minor clay associated with kerolite, stevensite, and sepiolite, commonly forming part of the clayey substrate linked to the growth of spherulites and shrubs. In XRD-based studies, it may be grouped with stevensite within Mg-smectite because distinguishing the two requires additional analytical work.

Continental breakup is a tectonic process that culminates in the final rupture of extended continental crust during late rifting to hyperextension, separating conjugate margins and initiating a new oceanic basin. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, this Early Cretaceous process helped establish the South Atlantic lacustrine basins and was uneven in time and space, so it is not necessarily represented by a single age-equivalent surface across the margin. On weak asymmetric margins, it may be recorded mainly in the most distal domains as an unconformity linked to final crustal rupture.

Sequence boundary is a stratigraphic surface that bounds adjacent depositional sequences by marking a break in sedimentation expressed as erosion, nondeposition, or truncation. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly corresponds to internal or regional unconformities separating stratigraphic units, recognizable in seismic data by angular truncations and, in some core-scale cycles, by clay-enriched horizons.

Syngenetic precipitation is a mineral precipitation process that takes place contemporaneously with sediment deposition, typically at or immediately below the sediment-water interface. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly refers to abiotic lacustrine precipitation of fascicular calcite crusts and stevensite controlled by shifts in water chemistry—such as pH, Mg and Ca activities, temperature, and pCO2—and expressed as encrustation or local replacement of stevensitic deposits.

Lula Field is a giant offshore pre-salt hydrocarbon field that occurs in the Santos Basin, Brazil, within Lower Cretaceous lacustrine carbonate reservoirs sealed by a thick salt interval. Discovered by the Tupi-1 well in 2006 and hosted on the Tupi High, it was the landmark multibillion-barrel discovery that proved the productivity and global significance of the Brazilian pre-salt play.

Carbonate build-up is a carbonate depositional body that forms localized positive relief by aggradational, in-place growth, commonly near fault-controlled structural highs in the Barra Velha interval and often associated with hydrothermal influence. In Brazilian Pre-Salt seismic data, it is typically expressed by chaotic to low-amplitude internal reflectors, intermediate to high acoustic impedance, and geometries onlapped and later overlain by evaporites. These bodies are commonly inferred to contain shrubby and spherulitic carbonates and to have among the highest porosity and permeability of the reservoir facies.

Karst is a dissolution-generated geological system that develops in soluble carbonate rocks through the percolation of meteoric or endogenous aqueous fluids, producing cavities, enlarged fractures, and other non-matrix voids. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates, karst is commonly controlled by faults and fracture networks and may form stratigraphically discordant high-permeability zones, although intense karstification can also generate collapse breccia and sediment infill that degrade reservoir quality.

Silica cement is a diagenetic cement that precipitates as silica minerals, mainly chalcedony and micro- to macrocrystalline quartz, lining and filling interparticle pores, vugs, and fractures in Pre-Salt carbonate reservoirs. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly occurs as pore-lining fringes or later pore-filling/drusy quartz, locally after earlier replacement phases, and may either partly preserve excess permeability or occlude pore space depending on its timing and abundance.

Mg-rich clay is a lacustrine evaporitic sedimentary facies that is composed of magnesium-rich clay minerals, commonly including stevensite, precipitated in shallow saline to alkaline lake environments. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, especially in the Barra Velha Formation, it commonly occurs around paleo-high flanks in moderate lake bathymetry, and its subsequent dissolution can create porosity and improve reservoir quality.

Microcrystalline silica is a fine-grained silica phase that replaces carbonate and Mg-clay components and locally cements pores in Brazilian Pre-Salt reservoir rocks. In the Barra Velha and Itapema formations, it commonly preserves host-rock textures during silicification, may occur in fabric-selective or non-selective patterns, and is generally associated with microporosity and with chalcedony and macrocrystalline quartz.

Shrubby spherulitestone is an in-situ lacustrine carbonate facies that is composed of more than 50% spherulites and calcite shrubs, with less than 10% mud, commonly arranged as poorly developed shrubs growing from spherulites in loose to tight frameworks. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it typically contains coarse- to fine-grained spherulites and very fine- to fine-grained shrubs, commonly shows an upward-coarsening trend with more frequent shrubs toward the top, and commonly preserves intergranular and fracture-related porosity.

Siliciclastic grain is a detrital sedimentary particle that consists of non-carbonate silicate minerals or volcanic lithic fragments derived from terrigenous sources. In the Brazilian pre-salt lacustrine carbonates, these grains commonly include quartz, feldspar, and mica, occur as minor mixed components introduced from rift-margin basement or volcanic sources by waves and currents, and their rarity indicates very limited siliciclastic input.

Sylvite is an evaporite mineral that consists of potassium chloride and precipitates from highly concentrated brines as a late-stage, highly soluble salt. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it occurs locally in the marine evaporitic Ariri Formation together with halite, anhydrite, carnallite, and tachyhydrite, overlying and sealing the Barra Velha reservoirs.

Talc-stevensite ooid is a coated grain that is composed predominantly of syngenetic magnesian clay minerals, chiefly stevensite with talc/kerolite, formed in alkaline lacustrine rift settings of the Brazilian Pre-Salt. It commonly occurs in stevensitic ooidal arenites and is characteristically prone to deformation, dissolution, and replacement or cementation by dolomite, quartz, silica, and locally calcite during diagenesis.

South Atlantic is an ocean basin that separates South America from Africa and whose Early Cretaceous opening generated the conjugate rifted margins associated with the Brazilian pre-salt. In the context of Brazilian carbonate reservoirs, the term commonly denotes the broader South Atlantic rift system, whose tectonic evolution, subsidence, lake hydrology, aridification, and later salt deposition controlled the development and preservation of pre-salt lacustrine carbonates.

Low-energy environment is a depositional setting that is characterized by weak hydrodynamic conditions, with little influence from waves or strong currents and minimal sediment reworking. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly corresponds to profundal or intermediate-depth lacustrine zones on sufficiently deep paleohighs, where laminites, mudstones, and spherulitestones develop and reservoir quality is often reduced by pore-filling calcite, mud, and Mg-silicate clays.

Piçarras Formation is a syn-rift lithostratigraphic unit that records the earliest siliciclastic and lacustrine deposition above the Camboriú volcanic sequence during Barremian rifting in the Santos Basin pre-salt. It typically comprises proximal alluvial-fan conglomerates and coarse to medium-grained sandstones, passing basinward into fine sandstones, siltstones, shales, siliciclastic laminites, and locally talc-stevensite and organic-rich dark shales.

Rift is an extensional tectonic setting that forms fault-bounded basins through active normal faulting and differential subsidence. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, the rift stage precedes continental breakup and is typically recorded by asymmetric wedges of growth strata and strong structural control on syn-rift siliciclastic, shale, and locally carbonate deposition.

Drift supersequence is a tectono-stratigraphic supersequence that records the passive-margin marine phase following Aptian evaporite deposition during the opening of the South Atlantic. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it is typically represented by shallow-marine platform carbonates of the Guarujá Formation and deeper-water sediments of the Itanhaém Formation, marking the transition from restricted lacustrine and evaporitic systems to fully marine conditions.

Microquartz is a diagenetic silica phase that consists of quartz crystals smaller than 20 μm and commonly fills inter-aggregate, interparticle, and vugular pores or replaces carbonate fabric in pre-salt carbonates. In the Santos Basin pre-salt, it is the most frequent silica phase associated with pervasive silicification and is generally interpreted as a late eogenetic cement, commonly occurring with chalcedony and megaquartz.

Fault system is a structural assemblage that groups faults with shared geometry, displacement, orientation, kinematic relationships, and relative age, and that collectively controls deformation and basin architecture. In the Santos Basin pre-salt, fault systems are primarily distinguished by the age of the growth strata and syn-rift sequences they influence, and they can be hierarchized into main systems and sub-systems that govern half-graben development, accommodation space, and subsidence through successive rift stages.

Post-rift supersequence is a tectonostratigraphic supersequence that records basin filling after the rift phase under dominant thermal subsidence, commonly as a sag-stage, aggradational succession that progressively heals residual relief on rift-related structures. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt of the Campos Basin, it overlies the regional Pre-Alagoas unconformity, includes the upper Lagoa Feia Group, is subdivided into Post-Rift I and Post-Rift II, and is capped by subaerial exposure and erosion preceding evaporite deposition.

Ultra-deep water is an offshore bathymetric setting that occurs at very large ocean depths, typically greater than about 1,500 m, above many giant Brazilian pre-salt reservoirs. In the pre-salt context, the term refers to the present-day Atlantic water depth of fields in the Santos and Campos basins, not to the original lacustrine depositional depth of the Aptian carbonate rocks.

Spherulitite is a carbonate rock that consists predominantly of spherulites, which are spherical to sub-spherical fibro-radial calcite aggregates. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, especially the Barra Velha Formation, it commonly occurs as spherulitic grainstone, packstone, or wackestone, and its spherulites typically show radial extinction and may be dolomitized, recrystallized, or locally silicified.

Bathymetry is a measure of subaqueous topography that quantifies water depth below lake level across a depositional surface. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates, bathymetry is commonly represented as positive depth values and is a key control on wave energy, wave base, carbonate growth rates, mud precipitation, and the distribution of facies in stratigraphic forward models.

Dark shale is a fine-grained shale that is dark because it contains significant organic matter and that, in the Brazilian pre-salt, commonly occurs interbedded with coquinas in the Itapema Formation. In the Santos Basin, these black to dark shales are important mainly as source rocks and, locally, as sealing intervals such as the highly radioactive Jiquiá Member at the top of the Itapema Formation.

Neobarremian is a chronostratigraphic interval that corresponds to the late part of the Barremian Stage in the Early Cretaceous. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it denotes the time span during which major subsalt reservoir rocks, especially those of the Itapema Formation and Barra Velha Formation, began to be deposited in lacustrine rift settings.

Oceanic crust is the mafic crustal domain that forms by seafloor spreading and accretion during continental breakup, marking the transition from rifting to a passive-margin drift stage. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt context, its generation records the onset of oceanic spreading, and the cooling of the newly formed crust drives the long-wavelength post-rift subsidence that controls basin evolution and reservoir burial.

Sururu Field is a Brazilian pre-salt oil field that is located on the Santos External High in the northern Santos Basin and contains Mid- to Late Aptian lacustrine carbonate reservoirs of the Lower Barra Velha Formation. Its reservoirs are dominantly fine-grained, mud-rich, low-permeability carbonates deposited on the crest of an NW-trending horst and compartmentalized by low-displacement normal faults and relay-ramp systems that create segmented structural highs and stratigraphic-structural traps.

Carbonate mud is a fine-grained carbonate sediment that occurs as matrix between larger grains or as discrete beds in Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly consists of micritic calcite and may also include clay minerals, dolomite, and silica, typically showing massive to millimetric laminated fabrics and local diagenetic replacement.

Reservoir architecture is a geological framework that describes the three-dimensional arrangement and connectivity of reservoir facies, stratigraphic surfaces, faults, and nonmatrix permeability features that control compartmentalization and fluid flow. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it is commonly analyzed at the scale of third-order sequences and is strongly influenced by depocenter geometry, facies distribution, fault juxtaposition against salt, and excess-permeability elements such as vugs, caves, fractures, and fault damage zones.

Volcanism is a geological process that involves the ascent, emplacement, and eruption of magma and associated gases at or near the Earth's surface. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt context, volcanism is important because syn-depositional eruptions and volcaniclastics can increase atmospheric CO2, contribute solutes to lacustrine waters, and help define rift-stage stratigraphic and paleoenvironmental conditions that influence carbonate deposition.

Diagenetic alteration is a post-depositional process that modifies the mineralogical, textural, and geochemical properties of carbonate sediments and rocks through fluid-rock interaction during shallow to deep burial. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly includes dissolution, dolomitization, silicification, pressure solution and cementation, and may involve hydrothermal overprints linked to faults or reactive freshwater influxes. These changes can overprint primary depositional fabrics and geochemical signatures and strongly control reservoir porosity and permeability.

Rift stage is a tectono-stratigraphic stage that records active crustal extension, normal faulting, and mechanically driven differential subsidence during basin formation. In the Brazilian pre-salt context, it comprises structurally controlled deposition in grabens and half-grabens, typically including coarse siliciclastics, shales, and lacustrine carbonate deposits arranged as growth strata before the rift-transition and post-rift stages.

Angular unconformity is a stratigraphic unconformity that truncates older tilted or deformed strata and is overlain by younger beds with a different, commonly more subparallel, orientation. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it typically marks the mid-pre-salt or Pre-Alagoas surface, separating divergent syn-rift lower pre-salt reflections from subparallel upper pre-salt deposits; it is most evident on structural highs and may pass laterally into a correlative conformity over rift depocentres.

Calcimudstone is a fine-grained carbonate rock that consists predominantly of clay-grade calcite smaller than 0.004 mm. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly occurs as dark micritic, massive to laminated laminae or beds, locally containing trace silt-size calcite, quartz, feldspar, and white mica and interlayered with calcisiltite and hybrid facies.

Hydraulic flow unit is a reservoir subdivision that comprises a zone or rock volume with sufficiently similar petrophysical and pore-throat characteristics to exhibit comparable fluid-flow behavior. In Brazilian pre-salt carbonates, HFUs are used to cluster intervals with similar grain size, texture, cementation, porosity, and permeability, helping represent reservoir heterogeneity and quality.

Neoproterozoic is the youngest era of the Proterozoic Eon that extends from about 1,000 to 541 million years ago. In the Brazilian pre-salt context, the term commonly refers to basement gneisses, fabrics, magmatism, and metamorphic-collisional events related to Brasiliano/Pan-African assembly, including deformation recorded broadly between about 650 and 490 Ma beneath and around the offshore basins.

Chemical compaction is a diagenetic compaction process that reduces pore space by pressure-solution of carbonate material at grain contacts and along stylolitic seams, followed by redistribution and cementation of the dissolved constituents. In Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates, it is mainly a mesodiagenetic process associated with stylolites and pore-filling calcite cements, which commonly diminishes primary porosity and permeability.

Dawsonite is an accessory authigenic carbonate mineral that consists of sodium aluminum carbonate hydroxide and occurs in Brazilian Pre-Salt reservoirs as a sparse late-diagenetic phase associated with fluorite, barite/celestite, sulfides, goyazite, and dolomite. In Aptian lacustrine carbonates of the Santos and Campos basins, it is typically detected by XRD or EDS in trace to very minor amounts, commonly below 5 wt.%, as part of the accessory mineral paragenesis.

Shallow lake is a lacustrine depositional environment that has low water depth relative to its areal extent, commonly producing a high area-to-depth ratio and, in Pre-Salt models, often corresponding to a hydrologically closed system strongly affected by evaporation and lake-level fluctuations. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, especially the Barra Velha Formation, this term denotes the very shallow setting interpreted for parts of the reservoir interval, where saline to alkaline waters favored carbonate facies such as shrubs, spherulites, and intraclast grainstones rather than deposition in a large deep lake.

Slope is an inclined margin surface that connects a structural or depositional high to an adjacent lower area in a lacustrine carbonate system. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, slopes are commonly imaged on seismic data as clinoforms and inclined reflectors along tilted fault blocks, ranging from low-angle dip slopes to steeper scarp slopes, and they may localize channels, collapse scars, and mass-transport deposits.

Microfracture is a small-scale brittle fracture that forms a narrow discontinuity within or across grains and carbonate fabrics at thin-section to micro-CT scale. In the Brazilian pre-salt carbonates, it commonly appears as isolated intragranular or fabric-cutting porosity, may be open, partially open, or cemented, and can locally increase permeability when microfractures are connected through the rock.

Growth framework porosity is a primary fabric-selective pore type that occupies the spaces between carbonate shrubs, spherulites, and their branches within the original depositional growth framework. In Brazilian Pre-Salt shrubstone-dominated reservoirs, it is commonly enhanced by dissolution but may be partially to completely occluded by dolomite or silica cements; in reworked calcirudites, it commonly occurs within porous shrub clasts.

Shallow marine environment is a depositional setting that develops in low-water-depth seawater, typically on shelves, ramps, or platform tops where waves, tides, evaporation, and periodic exposure strongly influence sedimentation. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt context, the term commonly refers to proposed transitional to marginal-marine conditions that may have succeeded shallow alkaline lacustrine systems and preceded widespread evaporite deposition.

Wackstone is a mud-supported carbonate facies that contains more than 10% grains, typically ostracod bioclasts and reworked fragments of shrubs, peloids, and spherulites, dispersed within a muddy matrix. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it is commonly fine grained, matrix supported, and either massive or plane-parallel laminated at core scale, with a finely laminated muddy matrix in thin section, and it commonly records low-energy intervals marking the return to more normal lacustrine conditions after stressful or storm-related events.

Claystone is a fine-grained sedimentary rock that is composed predominantly of clay-sized particles and, in the Brazilian Pre-Salt, commonly corresponds to stevensitic Mg-claystone within lacustrine carbonate successions. It typically occurs as laminated to massive, locally spherulite-rich facies and may also be reworked as intraclasts or as a clay matrix in hybrid carbonate rocks. In Pre-Salt reservoirs, its pore system and reservoir quality are commonly modified by dolomitization, silicification, and matrix dissolution.

Fascicular calcite crust is a lacustrine carbonate crust that consists of shrub-like, vertically to near-vertically growing fascicular-optic to radial-fibrous non-magnesian calcite aggregates encrusting the water-sediment interface. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly forms laminated to palisade crusts interbedded with Mg-silicates, siliciclastic mud, or peloidal laminae and constitutes one of the main reservoir facies of the sag section. Its fibrous crystalline fabric is interpreted mainly as an abiotic chemical precipitate, although it is commonly modified by recrystallization, dolomitization, and silicification.

Hybrid form is a transitional carbonate grain that combines morphological features of spherulites and crystal shrubs. In Brazilian pre-salt lacustrine carbonates, it typically has a spherical base, asymmetric cross-shaped figures under crossed polarized light, and elongate to branched growth perpendicular to bedding, reflecting precipitation under physicochemical conditions intermediate between low-energy spherulitic settings and more energetic, supersaturated shrubby settings.

Hydrocarbon reservoir is a subsurface rock body that contains and transmits accumulated hydrocarbons because it has sufficient porosity, permeability, and trapping conditions. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, these reservoirs are commonly lacustrine carbonate bodies whose quality and connectivity are strongly controlled by depositional facies, diagenetic alteration, fractures, vugs, and compartmentalization.

Atafona Formation is a syn-rift lithostratigraphic unit of the lower Lagoa Feia Group that is composed mainly of lacustrine arenites and siltstones rich in ooids of stevensite, kerolite, and other syngenetic magnesian layer silicates deposited in alkaline lakes. In the northern Campos Basin, it belongs to the Syn-rift I succession together with the Cabiúnas and Itabapoana formations, and it is commonly difficult to distinguish from the Itabapoana Formation in seismic and well-log data.

Cave is a meter-scale karstic cavity that forms by dissolution in carbonate rock and creates open nonmatrix pore space. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, caves are commonly recognized on borehole image logs as open cavities or borehole enlargements and are associated with severe to total drilling-fluid losses, very high permeability, and locally high production potential.

Matrix dissolution is a diagenetic process that selectively removes the fine-grained carbonate or Mg-clay matrix from a rock. In Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates, it commonly affects syngenetic Mg-clay or micritic matrices, creating matrix-dissolution porosity between dolomite rhombs and calcite or spherulitic components and generating laminar to vugular pore networks that can improve reservoir quality.

Tectonic quiescence is a tectonic regime that is marked by relatively low fault activity and minimal structural reorganization during deposition. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it typically refers to the sag-phase setting in which structural highs and lows maintained broadly stable stacking patterns, although faults reaching the base of the salt show that this quiescence was relative rather than absolute.

Paleohigh is a paleo-topographic high that remained relatively elevated during deposition, producing shallower bathymetry than adjacent flanks and basin lows. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, especially in the Barra Velha Formation, paleohighs are reconstructed from seismic horizons and lithology-controlled paleobathymetry and commonly localize shrubstone-dominated facies with fringes of spherulitestone and locally reworked deposits.

Camburi Group is a lithostratigraphic group that comprises Albian to Cenomanian post-salt marine siliciclastic and carbonate deposits of the drift phase above the Ariri evaporites in the Santos Basin. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt framework, it forms part of the passive-margin succession overlying the regional salt seal and marks the marine stage established after deposition of the pre-salt lacustrine reservoirs.

Laminated mudstone is a carbonate mudstone facies that displays fine to millimetric, commonly crinkly lamination formed by alternating calcitic-dolomitic mud layers with darker organic-rich, locally siliciclastic or dolomitic laminae. In the Brazilian pre-salt, especially the Barra Velha Formation, it commonly includes peloids or micropeloids, ostracods, local silica or chert laminae, and partial dolomitization, and it may preserve fenestral as well as intercrystalline-to-vugular or dissolution-related porosity.

Itamambuca Group is a stratigraphic group that forms the youngest, uppermost part of the drift-phase succession in the Santos Basin, deposited from the Danian to Recent in a marine setting. It records the final stage of post-rift basin deepening during Atlantic opening and is characterized by a prograding depositional system with well-developed slope clinoforms and basinward advance of the platform break, comprising siliciclastic and carbonate rocks above the pre-salt interval.

Namibe Basin is a South Atlantic marginal sedimentary basin that developed on the southwest African margin during Early Cretaceous rifting and sag and forms part of the conjugate Santos–Namibe basin system. In pre-salt studies, it is important because it preserves Aptian lacustrine carbonate successions and associated diagenetic and hydrothermal records that are commonly compared with those of the Brazilian Santos Basin.

Frade Group is a lithostratigraphic group that has been used locally for Lower Cretaceous continental to lacustrine deposits related to the syn-rift to early sag evolution of Brazil’s offshore marginal basins. In the context of Pre-Salt petroleum systems, it denotes strata that may include siliciclastic, coquina, and carbonate intervals associated with the buildup of the reservoir succession below the salt, although the term is less commonly used than Guaratiba Group or Lagoa Feia Group in regional studies.

Holocene is a geologic epoch that extends from the end of the Pleistocene to the present and represents the most recent interval of Earth history. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonate studies, Holocene deposits such as microbial flats, stromatolites, coquinas, and travertines are commonly used as modern analogs to interpret lacustrine and spring-related facies and processes.
