In situ facies is a carbonate facies that forms essentially in place by the precipitation of calcite shrubs and/or spherulites within muddy sediment, rather than by grain transport and reworking. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it is composed of microcrystalline calcite and clay-rich mud mixed with fascicular calcite shrubs and calcite spherulites, and it is commonly classified by the dominant component, such as shrubby or spherulitic facies, in relatively low-energy lacustrine zones.

Micropore is a submicron reservoir pore that, in Brazilian pre-salt carbonates, typically has a diameter of about 0.125 to 0.5 µm. It commonly occurs as dissolution-related intraparticle porosity within calcitic shrubs or as residual pore space between insoluble infillings in karst-modified cavities, and it is often associated with more intensely cemented, restricted pore systems.

Silica precipitation is a mineral-forming process that converts dissolved silica into authigenic chalcedony or quartz within pre-salt lacustrine carbonates, commonly as concordant layers, tabular to irregular bodies, or replacement of earlier Mg-clays and host carbonate fabrics. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it is commonly interpreted as penecontemporaneous with sedimentation or as early diagenetic (eogenetic/eodiagenetic), likely favored by freshening episodes and reduced lake alkalinity, although some disseminated silica formed during later diagenetic or hydrothermal stages.

Lake Tanganyika is a modern rift lake that serves as an analogue for the Lower Cretaceous pre-salt lacustrine system because it occupies a similar latitudinal setting and contains well-studied carbonate and stromatolite development in half-graben basins. In Brazilian pre-salt studies, it is used to constrain palaeohydrologic and geochemical parameters and to estimate stromatolite occurrence depths, which are commonly reported at about 10 to 60 m below lake level.

Abiotic precipitation is a chemical mineral-formation process that precipitates carbonate directly from supersaturated waters without direct mediation by microbial activity. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine system, it is associated with rapid precipitation from highly saturated solutions and can be promoted by CO2 loss during evaporation, as well as by changes in lake-water chemistry linked to magmatic CO2 input and hydrothermal activity.

Biofilm is a surface-attached microbial community that produces an organic matrix on sediment or carbonate substrates and influences mineral precipitation and the movement of sediment and pore fluids. In Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonates, biofilms are interpreted to favor calcite and early dolomite nucleation, template spherulitic and lamellar textures, and locally prevent sediment from entering or cement from filling shrubby fabrics.

Early Aptian is a geologic time interval that denotes the initial part of the Aptian Stage of the Early Cretaceous and, in the Brazilian Pre-Salt, corresponds to the late-rift to sag transition marked by deposition of Itapema coquinas and organic-rich mudstones, with some correlations placing the onset of major South Atlantic evaporite deposition in this interval. In the Santos and Campos basins, it is associated with decreasing tectonic activity, increasing thermal subsidence, and strata deposited immediately before the Pre-Alagoas Unconformity and overlying salt-bearing succession.

Uplift is a tectonic movement that raises a crustal block or structural high relative to adjacent areas. In the Brazilian pre-salt, uplift commonly affects fault footwalls or reactivated basement highs during rifting, reducing accommodation and inducing local lake-level retraction, erosion, and shallow-water carbonate deposition, thereby strongly controlling facies distribution and reservoir quality.

Rift section is a tectonostratigraphic interval that records the active extensional phase of a basin, including syn-rift volcanic rocks and overlying fluvial-lacustrine sediments deposited before the post-rift carbonates and evaporites. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it is divided into Syn-rift I and II, with the former corresponding to the Camboriú volcanic basement and the latter containing Piçarras source rocks and carbonate reservoir facies such as bioclastic grainstones, rudstones, stevensitic ooidal arenites, and dolostones.

Syn-rift phase is a tectono-stratigraphic stage that corresponds to active continental rifting, during which lithospheric stretching, normal faulting, and block rotation form grabens and half-grabens that govern deposition before continental breakup. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it is commonly subdivided into distinct rift phases and includes magmatic activity as well as the accumulation of volcanic rocks, organic-rich fluvial-lacustrine sediments, and early carbonate deposits such as those of the Camboriú, Piçarras, and Itapema formations.

Continental rifting is a tectonic process that stretches and thins continental lithosphere to generate normal faults, half-grabens, and accommodation space before continental breakup. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, especially in the Santos Basin, it began after deposition of the Camboriú Formation in the Hauterivian and controlled the development of isolated half-grabens, syn-rift stratigraphic sequences, and extensive lacustrine basins.

Intraclastic deposit is a reworked carbonate deposit that is composed predominantly of intraclasts eroded from earlier in situ lacustrine carbonates, especially spherulitic, fascicular shrub, shrubstone, and laminated facies, and redeposited within the pre-salt sag succession. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, these deposits commonly record multicycle reworking, are frequently intercalated with in situ deposits, and may occur as intraclastic grainstones or rudstones that form important reservoir intervals.

Structural domain is a structural subdivision of a basin that is distinguished from adjacent areas by a coherent fault pattern, geometry, and deformation style. In the Brazilian pre-salt, structural domains commonly include horsts, grabens, half-grabens, or deep and shallow faulted sectors, and they control depocenter distribution, accommodation-zone development, sedimentary facies, reservoir quality, and fluid connectivity.

Relay ramp is a fault-related transfer structure that forms between overlapping or stepping normal-fault segments to transfer displacement through an inclined intervening zone. In the Brazilian pre-salt, relay ramps are commonly associated with basement-controlled horst-graben architecture and accommodation zones, and their degree of preservation or rupture influences fault linkage, transverse fracturing and folding, and reservoir compartmentalization.

Fracture zone is a structural rock domain that contains a concentrated network of fractures and therefore exhibits higher fracture intensity than the surrounding host rock. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, fracture zones are commonly fault-related, occurring around major faults, near fault tips, or in soft-linkage areas between adjacent faults, where they strongly influence non-matrix porosity and fluid flow in carbonate reservoirs.

Fluid flow is a reservoir transport process that describes the movement of fluids through the interconnected pore and fracture system of a rock in response to pressure gradients and fluid properties. In Brazilian pre-salt carbonates, it is mainly controlled by porosity, permeability, pore-throat geometry, mineralogy, texture, fractures, and stratigraphic heterogeneities, which can create vertical barriers and horizontal flow corridors and thereby govern production behavior.

Paleotopography is a reconstructed topographic surface that represents the relief and water-depth configuration of the depositional substrate at a specific geologic time. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it is commonly derived from seismic horizons and paleo-bathymetric normalization and used as a boundary condition in stratigraphic simulations, while also controlling facies distribution, structural highs, and zones prone to subaerial exposure and non-matrix porosity development.

Lithology is a rock-descriptive attribute that identifies a rock or reservoir interval by its mineral composition, texture, fabric, and internal structures. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, lithology is used to distinguish carbonate types such as shrubstone, spherulstone, mudstone, calcarenite, and calcirudite, and it is commonly integrated with core, image logs, and conventional well logs because it strongly influences pore systems and reservoir quality.

Meteoric water is a natural water that originates as atmospheric precipitation and, after runoff or infiltration, circulates as surface water or shallow groundwater. In Brazilian Pre-Salt lacustrine carbonate systems, it is typically more dilute and mildly acidic than lake water, so its influx can freshen the basin, lower salinity and alkalinity, and influence early diagenesis. After water-rock interaction, meteoric fluids may also become carbonate-saturated and feed fault-controlled spring or travertine systems.

Drift super-sequence is a tectonostratigraphic super-sequence that records the passive-margin stage of basin evolution after the post-rift evaporitic interval, marked by Atlantic opening, thermal subsidence, and fully marine sedimentation. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt of the Santos Basin, it is represented mainly by shallow-marine platform carbonates of the Guarujá Formation and deeper-water sediments, including siliciclastics, of the Itanhaém Formation. This succession reflects the transition from restricted lacustrine and evaporitic systems to open-marine deposition, locally accompanied by platform drowning.

Arid climate is a climatic regime that is defined by evaporation exceeding precipitation (P < E), producing a net water deficit and evaporative concentration of lake waters. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, this condition is linked to reduced fluvial input, commonly increased aeolian dust contribution, higher pH, and the precipitation of Mg-clays, spherulites, shrubs, and eventually evaporites such as the overlying salt sequences.

Illite is a potassium-rich non-expanding clay mineral that occurs in Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates as a minor phyllosilicate constituent, commonly as discrete illite or interstratified illite/smectite. In the Santos Basin it is typically detected in low abundances by XRD and may represent detrital clay or burial-related transformation products of earlier clay minerals.

Rift super-sequence is a tectono-stratigraphic super-sequence that groups the syn-rift deposits accumulated during active extensional faulting and fault-controlled lacustrine basin development in the Brazilian Pre-Salt. In the Santos Basin, it is mainly represented by the Camboriú, Piçarras, and Itapema formations, comprising basalts, continental siliciclastics, lacustrine coquinas, organic-rich shales, and locally talc-stevensite ooid-bearing intervals, with some interpretations also including the basal wedge of the Barra Velha Formation.

Muddy spherulitestone is an in situ spherulitic carbonate facies that contains about 70–90% spherulites and mud, with rounded, well- to moderately sorted spherulite grains embedded in a muddy matrix or arranged in centimetric spherulite-rich layers interlaminated with mud. It commonly occurs as coarse- to fine-grained, loosely to densely packed frameworks in Mg-silicate or carbonate mud matrices, and densely packed layers may show interdigitated grain contacts and deformation of the spherulites.

Passive-margin basin is a sedimentary basin that develops along a continental margin after rifting and continental breakup, with post-rift thermal subsidence controlling its drift-stage sedimentation. In the Brazilian pre-salt province, basins such as Santos and Campos evolved into passive-margin basins after the Early Cretaceous opening of the South Atlantic, accumulating Albian shallow-marine platform carbonates followed by deeper-water sediments.

Thrombolite is a microbialite that exhibits a clotted, commonly cryptocrystalline internal fabric instead of the well-defined lamination typical of stromatolites. In the Aptian Brazilian pre-salt, thrombolites are rare in situ microbial carbonates and are classified by their structure alongside stromatolites, dendrolites, and leiolites.

Tachyhydrite is a hydrated chloride evaporite mineral that is composed of calcium and magnesium chlorides and occurs locally within the Ariri Formation salt sequence of the Brazilian Pre-Salt. In the Santos Basin, it is a minor accessory evaporite associated with halite, anhydrite, carnallite, and sylvite, indicating highly concentrated brine conditions during Aptian salt deposition.

Interparticle pore is a pore space that occurs between adjacent grains, intraclasts, or other particles in a carbonate rock. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it is especially common in reworked facies such as calcirudites and calcarenites, where dissolution may enlarge it and bedding may organize it into stratified, concordant porosity. When these pores remain open and connected they commonly support high permeability, but they may also be partially or completely occluded by silica, dolomite, or anhydrite cement.

Pore connectivity is a petrophysical property that expresses the degree to which pores in a rock are interconnected to form continuous pathways for fluid flow. In Brazilian pre-salt carbonates, it is a key control on permeability because much of the connected network may reside in pores below CT-scan resolution, whereas dolomitization and silicification can generate closed or isolated pores that reduce connectivity.

Fluorite is a halide mineral that consists of calcium fluoride and, in Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates, commonly occurs as a minor secondary phase replacing constituents and lining or filling pores, especially dissolution-enhanced pore margins. In the Santos Basin, its presence is typically interpreted as a product of hydrothermal alteration and localized hydrothermal fluid circulation affecting the carbonate reservoir.

Intrusive igneous rock is an igneous rock that forms when magma is emplaced within pre-existing strata and crystallizes below the surface. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, especially in the Mero/Libra area, these bodies are mainly Santonian/Campanian alkaline intrusions that may cut surrounding rocks or occur concordant with sedimentary layering, including near the top of the Barra Velha Formation. They are critical to reservoir characterization because they reduce effective reservoir volume, may act as flow barriers or fractured high-permeability intervals, and can induce hydrothermal alteration that commonly tightens adjacent carbonates.

Magnesite is a magnesium carbonate mineral (MgCO3) that occurs in the Brazilian Pre-Salt mainly as a secondary diagenetic phase replacing Mg-clays and filling shrinkage pores. In Aptian Santos Basin carbonates, it is typically found as lamellar aggregates in Mg-claystones with spherulites and tends to be more abundant where Mg-clay replacement is more intense.

Intracrystalline porosity is a secondary pore type that develops within individual crystals or crystal interiors through partial dissolution of minerals such as calcite or dolomite. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates, it commonly results from dissolution of pore-filling calcite cement, dolomite rhombs, or shrub and fascicular calcite fabrics, and it may provide measurable porosity even where little other petrographic pore space is visible.

Santonian is a Late Cretaceous geologic age and chronostratigraphic stage that, in the Santos Basin context, designates Upper Cretaceous intervals and events recognized in postsalt reservoir successions and regional magmatism. In Brazilian pre-salt studies, the term is used both for Santonian-age postsalt turbiditic reservoirs and for a Santonian igneous phase that has been interpreted as spatially related to dolomitization in pre-salt carbonates.

Accommodation zone is a zone of distributed deformation that accommodates strain between poorly connected, overlapping, or unsuccessfully linked rift fault segments, commonly expressed by opposing dip domains and increasing bed dips. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt syn-rift, accommodation zones function as intrabasin transfer or bypass areas that segment structural domains and influence depocentre continuity, facies distribution, and reservoir quality in lacustrine carbonates.

Berriasian is a chronostratigraphic stage and geochronologic age that defines the earliest part of the Cretaceous Period. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt context, it refers to an early syn-rift interval that predates the main Barremian–Aptian deposition of the lacustrine carbonate reservoirs such as the Itapema and Barra Velha successions.

Carbonate shale is a fine-grained fissile sedimentary rock that contains a substantial carbonate component within laminated shale, typically deposited in low-energy deeper-water parts of a carbonate system. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly becomes more abundant basinward from slope carbonates into basinal or profundal settings and generally behaves as a tight, nonreservoir to sealing facies that can compartmentalize adjacent carbonate reservoirs.

Anticline is a structural fold that arches rock layers upward so that its flanks dip away from a hinge or axial zone. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, anticlines commonly form elongated structural highs identifiable in seismic data and can influence facies distribution, fracture development, fluid migration, and hydrocarbon trapping.

Lapa Field is an offshore pre-salt petroleum field that is located in the central Santos Basin and contains a carbonate reservoir charged with good-quality light oil beneath the evaporite section. It was discovered by Petrobras in 2007 as the Carioca area, later renamed Lapa upon commercial declaration, and became the third pre-salt field to enter production in the Santos Basin.

Asthenospheric uplift is a tectonic uplift that is driven by upwelling of the asthenospheric mantle and associated thermal anomaly beneath a thinning continental lithosphere. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt rift system, it refers to an early extensional-stage doming that accompanies lithospheric stretching, helps initiate fault-controlled depocenters and half-grabens, and may locally be linked to plume-related heating and CO2 degassing.

Carbonate dissolution is a diagenetic process that removes carbonate minerals from carbonate rocks through interaction with undersaturated or acidic fluids, generating secondary pores. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it commonly occurs during both eodiagenesis and mesodiagenesis, affecting features such as grainstones, shrubs, Mg-clays, and diagenetic minerals through meteoric exposure, tectonically controlled fluid flow, and locally hydrothermal CO2- or H2S-bearing fluids. Although it is the main mechanism for forming secondary porosity, its overall increase in pore volume and reservoir quality may be limited.

Lake is a continental standing body of water that occupies a tectonically controlled depression and forms the lacustrine depositional setting in which water depth, accommodation, hydrodynamics, and chemistry regulate sedimentation. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, relative lake-level rises and falls mark phases of deepening and shallowing that strongly control the distribution of carbonate facies such as stromatolites, spherulitites, grainstones, and laminites.

Depositional model is a conceptual sedimentological framework that reconstructs the depositional environments, processes, and facies distribution responsible for a sedimentary succession. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates, it commonly relates reservoir facies to variations in lake level and hydrodynamic energy, distinguishing shallow, reworked, higher-permeability facies such as intraclastic and oolitic grainstones from deeper, lower-energy lacustrine deposits and helping predict the distribution of high-quality reservoirs.

Weathering is a near-surface alteration process that modifies exposed carbonate rocks through chemical, physical, and biogenic reactions during subaerial exposure, commonly obliterating the original rock texture. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it is expressed as weathering profiles or paleosol-like intervals developed on exposed shallow-lake or structural-high deposits, typically showing fine-grained granular fabric, possible root marks, common dolomitization and silicification, and locally sharp contacts with the underlying unweathered rock.

Basement rock is the pre-sedimentary geological substrate that forms the structural floor beneath the Brazilian pre-salt succession. In the Santos Basin, it comprises mainly Precambrian crystalline rocks such as granitoids and gneisses, and, in economic-stratigraphic terms, may also include the Camboriú Formation basalts that overlie the crystalline basement unconformably; its composition and inherited fabric strongly influence rifting, basement highs, and the distribution of overlying lacustrine carbonate reservoirs.

Acoustic impedance is an elastic property of the formation that equals the product of bulk density and P-wave velocity. In Brazilian Pre-Salt carbonates, it is commonly computed from density and sonic logs or used in seismic interpretation, and where matrix composition is relatively uniform its variations are largely controlled by total porosity, so low-impedance zones can indicate reservoir facies such as carbonate mounds.

Tholeiitic basalt is a mafic volcanic rock that crystallizes from tholeiitic magma, typically low in alkalis relative to silica, and in the Brazilian pre-salt occurs as Early Cretaceous flood or subaqueous basalt flows underlying the sedimentary succession or interbedded with the Itapema and Barra Velha formations. In the Santos and Campos basins, these basalts are commonly linked to the Camboriú/Cabiúnas magmatic event and are reservoir-relevant because they may constitute the economic basement and locally act as flow barriers or, where intensely fractured, high-permeability conduits.

Carbonate ramp is a carbonate platform that has a low-angle, gently sloping profile and facies belts that grade from backshore or shoreface into offshore and profundal settings without an abrupt shelf margin. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, its facies distribution is strongly controlled by fair-weather and storm-wave hydrodynamic zones and may also be influenced by hemigraben subsidence and fault reactivation.

Transitional environment is a depositional setting that lies between two adjacent environments and is characterized by intermediate water-energy or physicochemical conditions. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly refers to facies belts such as slope or beach zones between shallow and deeper lacustrine settings, where moderate energy and mixed deposits such as grainstones, spherulites, and hybrid fabrics can develop.

Aggradation is a stratigraphic stacking pattern that builds carbonate deposits upward by predominantly vertical accumulation as accommodation is created, rather than mainly by basinward progradation. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it is expressed by the vertical stacking of seismic facies and the growth of mounded marginal build-ups or promontories, commonly linked to subsidence on rotating fault blocks and locally accompanied by backstepping or asymmetric margin growth.

Granite is an intrusive igneous rock that crystallizes slowly at depth and is composed predominantly of quartz and feldspars, with minor micas and accessory minerals. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, granite commonly refers to part of the crystalline basement underlying the Aptian carbonate succession, where its fracturing, weathering, or local reworking can influence sediment supply and reservoir architecture.

Pre-salt carbonate is a lacustrine carbonate rock that was deposited in the Lower Cretaceous pre-evaporitic interval beneath the South Atlantic salt, forming the main reservoir facies of the Brazilian Pre-Salt. It is typically composed of limestone, dolomite, and silica with frequent magnesian clays such as stevensite, and occurs in highly variable facies including bioclastic grainstones and rudstones, fascicular calcite crusts, spherulitic deposits, and reworked intraclastic carbonates. Its reservoir quality is commonly highly heterogeneous because of strong facies variability and complex diagenetic overprinting, including dolomitization and silicification.

Mound is a carbonate buildup that forms a positive-relief, commonly isolated or platform-margin body through shrub-rich carbonate precipitation, typically linked to hydrothermal fluid discharge along faults in lacustrine Pre-Salt settings. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, mounds are seismic facies composed mainly of shrubstone and shrubby spherulitestone, formed in intermediate to shallow sublittoral zones, locally exposed subaerially, and commonly enriched in silica and uranium.

Passive margin basin is a sedimentary basin that develops on a tectonically quiescent continental margin after continental breakup and ocean opening. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, exemplified by the Santos Basin, it is related to the Neocomian breakup of Gondwana and typically records rift, post-rift or sag, and drift successions from continental to transitional and marine environments.

Turonian is a Late Cretaceous geologic age and stratigraphic stage that lies between the Cenomanian and Coniacian stages. In the Santos Basin postsalt succession, Cenomanian–Turonian marine black shales of the lower Itajaí-Açu Formation are important source rocks that generated hydrocarbons after reaching peak thermal maturity in deeper areas influenced by salt withdrawal.

Rift fault is a normal fault that develops during crustal extension in a rift basin and accommodates syn-rift deformation by generating displacement, subsidence, and structural compartmentalization. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, rift faults commonly occur as conjugate fault families that control sediment accommodation space and basement or base-salt compartmentalization, and they may later be reactivated during transtensional or transpressional deformation, influencing reservoir architecture and fracture-related porosity.

Footwall is the fault-bounded rock block that lies below an inclined fault plane. In the Brazilian pre-salt rift setting, uplift of the footwall along normal faults commonly generates structural highs, promotes erosion and coarse-clastic input, and influences lake-level retraction, facies distribution, and reservoir quality.

Spherulitic carbonate is a carbonate rock or facies that is dominated by spherical to elliptical carbonate spherulites, typically 0.1-5 mm in diameter, composed of fibroradial calcite around a micritic, microsparitic, or siliciclastic nucleus and commonly embedded in a clay-rich or organic-rich muddy matrix. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it occurs as spherulitestones, packstones, or grainstones, may form in situ or be reworked, and is commonly linked to biologically influenced precipitation in low-energy lacustrine settings. Dissolution of spherulite nuclei can generate moldic porosity that affects reservoir quality.

Economic basement is a syn-rift volcanic basement interval that consists mainly of Hauterivian basaltic rocks of the Camboriú Formation forming the base of the Santos Basin pre-salt succession. In seismic interpretation it is commonly recognized by a high-amplitude reflector or unconformity caused by the strong impedance contrast with overlying Piçarras siliciclastics, and its lower boundary separates it from the deeper acoustic basement.

Rift sequence is a tectonostratigraphic unit that records volcanic and sedimentary deposition during basin-forming crustal extension and normal faulting, typically within fault-controlled horsts, grabens, and half-grabens. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it corresponds to the Early Cretaceous syn-rift succession, commonly including basal basalts, overlying lacustrine siliciclastics, bioclastic carbonates such as coquinas, and associated source-rock mudstones. It may be subdivided into lower and upper rift intervals or multiple rift phases by intra-rift unconformities and seismic reflector terminations.

Magnesium clay is a Mg-rich clay mineral assemblage that occurs syngenetically in alkaline, saline lacustrine pre-salt carbonates and is commonly represented by stevensite and kerolite. In Brazilian Pre-Salt reservoirs, it typically forms massive or laminated aggregates associated with calcitic spherulites, and because it is chemically unstable it is commonly dolomitized, silicified, dissolved, or replaced by calcite during diagenesis.

Cenomanian is a Late Cretaceous geochronologic age and corresponding chronostratigraphic stage that spans approximately 100.5 to 93.9 million years ago. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt context, the term is mainly used to date younger post-salt marine successions that overlie the Aptian lacustrine carbonate reservoirs rather than the reservoir interval itself.

Tectonic activity is a geodynamic process that produces faulting, deformation, and fault reactivation, creating accommodation space and structural relief that govern sediment deposition. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it is most intense during the rift stage and generally decreases into the sag/post-rift stage, yet it can still locally control lake geometry, depocenter distribution, carbonate facies development, and reservoir thickness.

Microcrystalline quartz is a diagenetic quartz phase that is composed of crystals smaller than about 20 μm and typically replaces carbonate grains and fabric or fills inter-aggregate, interparticle, and vugular pore spaces. In the Brazilian pre-salt, it is the major silica phase associated with pervasive silicification, commonly replacing ooids and peloids and occurring together with chalcedony and macrocrystalline quartz.

Macrocrystalline quartz is a diagenetic silica cement that precipitates as relatively coarse quartz crystals, typically forming mosaic or drusy fillings in pore centers and locally replacing carbonate grains or bioclasts. In the Brazilian Pre-Salt, it commonly postdates microcrystalline quartz and chalcedony and is therefore interpreted as a late silicification phase that fills interparticle, intraparticle, and dissolution porosity, especially in bivalve bioclasts and crustone-related pores.

Búzios Field is a supergiant pre-salt oil and gas field that hosts Barremian–Aptian lacustrine carbonate reservoirs in the northern Santos Basin offshore southeastern Brazil. Located on the Santos Basin Outer High in ultra-deep water about 180 km off Rio de Janeiro, it is one of the world’s largest offshore hydrocarbon accumulations and a major producer from the Barra Velha and Itapema formations.
